the-tomb-of-our-lord.name: The tomb of Our Lord
the-tomb-of-our-lord.title: The Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem
the-tomb-of-our-lord.summary: A relic from the sepulchre in Jerusalem where the Gospels say Jesus was buried and the women found the tomb empty. Constantine had the site uncovered in 325 or 326, and many historians think it may well be the right place, though it cannot be proved. It has no formal patronage, but for monks who bury their brothers, the empty tomb is why death can be faced calmly.
life: The label “Ex Sepul. D.N.” means “from the sepulchre of Our Lord”. The Gospels say that Jesus was buried in a new tomb cut in the rock, in a garden near the place where he was crucified, and that on the third day the women found it empty. There is no relic of his body. A relic like this one is a tiny chip of stone from the tomb, or a piece of cloth or stone touched to it, carried home by pilgrims.

In 325 or 326 the Emperor Constantine had Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem uncover the site. Eusebius of Caesarea, who wrote at the time, says that a pagan temple had been built over it in the 2nd century, and that when the temple was pulled down a tomb cut in the rock was found beneath. Constantine built the first Church of the Holy Sepulchre around it, and it was dedicated in 335. The church was burned and rebuilt more than once. In 1009 the Caliph al-Hakim ordered the tomb itself hacked down almost to the bedrock. What pilgrims see today is a small shrine, the Edicule, rebuilt in 1810 over what remains.

Many historians and archaeologists think it may well be the right place. It lay outside the city walls in Jesus' day, as a tomb had to, and the Christians of Jerusalem seem to have remembered it through the two centuries before Constantine. It cannot be proved. When the Edicule was restored in 2016, the marble slab over the burial bench was lifted for the first time in centuries, and mortar found beneath it was dated to the middle of the 4th century, which fits Constantine's work.

The Church claims no more for such a relic than that it comes from, or has touched, that place. What it points to is the empty tomb itself. Christ died, was buried and rose, and Christians hope to rise with him.
patronage: No formal patronage. Pilgrims pray there for faith in the Resurrection, for their dead, and for a holy death
The Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, which supports the Church in the Holy Land, takes its name from it
why_here: Br. Joseph Zoettl built many of the Ave Maria Grotto's miniatures to show the Holy Land to people who would never see it. A relic from the tomb in Jerusalem does the same thing in a smaller way. It brings a faraway holy place close to people in Alabama who will likely never stand in it.

It also belongs beside the abbey's cemetery and its infirmary. The monks of St. Bernard are buried on their own grounds, and the old and sick among them are cared for at home until they die. The empty tomb is the reason a monastery can face death calmly. Every grave in the monks' cemetery waits on what happened in that garden in Jerusalem.
the-tomb-of-our-lord.relic: One relic: “Ex Sepul. D.N.” (from the sepulchre of Our Lord), at the centre of the large oval of about ten relics in the velvet case, beside “Domus Laur.” (IMG_4894–4899).

the-holy-nail.name: The Holy Nail
the-holy-nail.title: Relic of the Passion
the-holy-nail.feast: None of its own on today's calendar; the Passion is kept on Good Friday
the-holy-nail.summary: A relic of the nails of the Crucifixion, almost certainly a cloth or copy touched to a venerated nail rather than a piece of one. St. Ambrose wrote in 395 that St. Helena found the nails with the Cross, but there are more such nails than there could have been. It has no formal patronage and recalls Christ's death, a fitting relic among the abbey's woodworkers who build altars.
life: The label “Ex S. Clavo D.N.I.C.” means “from the Holy Nail of Our Lord Jesus Christ”. The nails are in the Gospels. After the Resurrection, St. Thomas says he will not believe unless he sees in Jesus' hands “the print of the nails” (John 20:25).

The oldest written account of the nails being found is by St. Ambrose of Milan, in his funeral sermon for the Emperor Theodosius in 395. He says that St. Helena, the mother of Constantine, found the Cross in Jerusalem and the nails with it, and that she had one made into a bit for her son's horse and another set into his crown. In later centuries many churches came to keep a nail venerated as one of these. Among them are Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome, the cathedrals of Milan and Trier, and the Iron Crown of Lombardy at Monza, whose inner band was said to be beaten from a nail. There are more of these nails than there could have been at the Crucifixion, and the Church has never ruled on any of them.

A relic like this one is almost certainly not a piece of such a nail. It is a cloth or a small copy touched to one of them, or at most a filing from it. In the Middle Ages a feast of the Holy Lance and Nails was kept in some places, especially in the German lands, but it is not on today's calendar.
The Church allows these relics to be honored for what they point to, the death of Christ. The honor goes to him, not to the iron.
patronage: No formal patronage. Christians pray before relics of the Passion in sorrow for sin and in thanks for Christ's death
why_here: Jesus grew up in a carpenter's house and died nailed to wood. The abbey has long had craftsman monks, builders and carvers, and its woodworkers still make altars, pulpits, pews and doors. Every altar they build is a table for the Mass, where the sacrifice this nail recalls is made present. It is a fitting relic to keep among men who work with wood and iron, and a plain reminder to the Prep's students during Lent and Holy Week of what Good Friday cost.
the-holy-nail.relic: One relic on the linen board: “Ex S. Clavo D.N.I.C.” (from the Holy Nail of Our Lord Jesus Christ; IMG_4940).

the-holy-house-of-loreto.name: The Holy House of Loreto
the-holy-house-of-loreto.title: The house of the Annunciation, as tradition holds
the-holy-house-of-loreto.summary: The shrine at Loreto in Italy keeps a small stone room said to be the house at Nazareth where the angel Gabriel came to Mary. The story that angels carried it there is legend, and how the stones arrived cannot be proved. Our Lady of Loreto is patron of aviators (Benedict XV, 1920), a fitting patron for Prep students who fly to school from across the country and abroad.
life: Since the 15th century the shrine at Loreto, on Italy's Adriatic coast, has kept a small room of stone said to be the house at Nazareth where Mary lived, where the angel Gabriel came to her, and where Jesus grew up. It has only three walls. It stands inside a large basilica, wrapped in a carved marble screen begun in the early 1500s, and pilgrims have come to it for more than five hundred years. The name of the town is said to come from the laurel grove (lauretum) where the house came to rest.

The pious tradition is that angels carried the house from Nazareth in 1291, when the last crusader strongholds in the Holy Land fell. They set it down first at Trsat in Dalmatia, and then in 1294 near Loreto. This is legend, not history. Some historians think instead that the stones were brought by ship from the Holy Land in the time of the Crusades, possibly by a family named Angeli, and that the name may lie behind the story of angels. Neither account can be proved.

The popes have honored the shrine for centuries. The Litany of Loreto, the long list of Mary's titles still prayed today, takes its name from the shrine where it was sung. Because of the story of the flight through the air, Pope Benedict XV named Our Lady of Loreto patron of aviators in 1920. In 2019 Pope Francis added her memorial on 10 December to the General Roman Calendar.

“Domus Laur.” means “the house of Loreto”. Relics of this kind are usually a crumb of its stone or mortar, or a piece of cloth touched to its walls. Whatever the history of the stones, what the shrine honors is the Incarnation, God made man in an ordinary home.
why_here: The Ave Maria Grotto is itself a collection of holy places brought far from home. Br. Joseph Zoettl built many miniatures of the Holy Land and of Rome so that people in Alabama could see them. The Holy House, if the tradition is right, is the most famous holy place ever to have traveled.

Its patronage fits the Prep as well. Students come from across the country and from abroad, and many of them fly to school and home again. Our Lady of Loreto is the patron of everyone in the air. And the house she guards is the home where Jesus grew up and obeyed his parents. That is a good thing to pray for on behalf of boarders living away from their own homes, and for the monastery, which is itself meant to be a household.
the-holy-house-of-loreto.relic: One relic: “Domus Laur.” (the house of Loreto), at the centre of the large oval of about ten relics in the velvet case, beside “Ex Sepul. D.N.” (IMG_4894–4899).

the-tomb-of-our-lady.name: The tomb of the Blessed Virgin Mary
the-tomb-of-our-lady.title: The tomb in the Kidron Valley
the-tomb-of-our-lady.summary: A relic from the tomb of the Virgin Mary in the Kidron Valley at Jerusalem, honored there since at least the 5th century. There are no relics of her body, since the Church teaches she was taken up body and soul into heaven. Christians pray there for a holy death, and the relic suits monks who keep the Ave Maria Grotto in her honor and bury their brothers in hope.
life: “Ex sepulchro” means “from the tomb”. This is not a relic of Mary's body, and that is not an accident. That Mary was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory is dogma, defined by Pope Pius XII in Munificentissimus Deus in 1950. The Church teaches that no bodily relics of her exist. Whether she died before her Assumption was deliberately left undefined. That she did, the “Dormition” or falling asleep, is the older and more common view, but it remains theological opinion.

Two places have claimed her last days. The Jerusalem tradition is older and stronger. From at least the 5th century a church stood over a tomb in the Kidron Valley, at the foot of the Mount of Olives beside Gethsemane. Writings of about the same time tell how the apostles buried her there and later found the tomb empty. Those stories are legend, but they show where Christians in Jerusalem honored her tomb. The claim of Ephesus, in Turkey, is much later and rests largely on the visions of a 19th-century German nun, Bl. Anne Catherine Emmerich.

The church over the tomb was destroyed and rebuilt more than once. In the time of the Crusades, Benedictine monks kept an abbey there, St. Mary of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and Queen Melisende of Jerusalem was buried in it in 1161. After 1187 the upper church was pulled down, but the underground church survived. Pilgrims still go down a long stairway to a small chapel cut around the rock bench where her body is said to have lain. Today it is in the care of the Greek Orthodox and the Armenians, and Muslims come to pray there too.
What pilgrims could bring home was a fragment from that tomb or a cloth touched to it. It is a relic of the place, a witness that her body was laid there and is no longer there.
patronage: No formal patronage of its own. Christians pray there for a holy death and in hope of the resurrection of the body
why_here: The abbey's best-known work bears her name. The Ave Maria Grotto, dedicated in 1934, was Br. Joseph Zoettl's life's work in her honor, and visitors still come to it from far away. A relic from her tomb belongs naturally to the monks who keep it.

There is a Benedictine thread as well. For a time in the Middle Ages monks who lived by the same Rule as St. Bernard's kept watch over this very tomb. And the feast it points to is the hope of every Christian death. The monks bury their brothers in their own cemetery and care for the old and sick in their infirmary. The empty tomb of Mary says that the body laid in the ground is not the end of the story.
the-tomb-of-our-lady.relic: Two relics in the velvet case: “Ex Sepul. [B.] V. M.” beside St. John the Baptist (IMG_4892, 4893), and “Ex Sepul. V. M.” at the centre of a square theca with St. Joseph, St. Anne, St. Peter and St. Paul (IMG_4901, 4902).

our-ladys-garment.name: Our Lady's garment
our-ladys-garment.title: Relic of the Virgin's clothing
our-ladys-garment.summary: A relic of the Virgin Mary's clothing, most likely a thread or cloth touched to a relic such as the veil of Chartres or the girdle of Prato, none of which can be traced back to Mary herself. By old custom at Chartres, mothers awaiting a child have sought her protection. It suits a monastery that does its own tailoring, and Prep families expecting a child.
life: “Ex Veste B. M. V.” means “from the garment of the Blessed Virgin Mary”. The Church teaches as dogma, defined by Pope Pius XII in 1950, that Mary was taken up body and soul into heaven at the end of her earthly life. So there are no relics of her body. Relics of Mary are of things she is said to have worn or touched, or of her tomb.

The best known are the veil at Chartres Cathedral in France and the girdle, or belt, at Prato in Italy. The veil was given to Chartres by the Emperor Charles the Bald in 876. When the cathedral burned in 1194 the veil was found unharmed, and people took that as a sign to rebuild, which gave us the cathedral that stands today. The Prato girdle has a later legend. It says that Mary let it fall to St. Thomas as she was taken up into heaven, and that a merchant brought it from the Holy Land in the 12th century. In Constantinople, a robe of the Virgin was kept for centuries in the church of Blachernae, and the Eastern churches still keep a feast of it on 2 July.

None of these can be traced back to Mary herself, and some of the stories are plainly legend. Small threads or pieces of cloth touched to such relics were given out over the centuries, and a relic like this one is most likely of that kind. The Church makes no claim that a given thread is truly from her clothing. What it honors is the woman the relic recalls, and the care Christians have long asked of her.
patronage: mothers awaiting a child (by long custom at Chartres, where cloths touched to the veil were given to them)
Mary's protection, pictured in art as her mantle spread over those who pray to her
why_here: Monks wear a habit, and the abbey still does its own tailoring. A relic of Mary's clothing suits a house where men are given the clothes of their vocation and keep them mended. The abbey also lives beside the Ave Maria Grotto, built in her honor, and asks her protection as a family would.

The old custom at Chartres gives it a place in the Prep's prayers too. Among the school's families and teachers there are always mothers expecting a child. Those are good prayers to bring before this relic.
our-ladys-garment.relic: One relic on the linen board: “Ex Veste B. M. V.” (from the garment of the Blessed Virgin Mary; IMG_4923).

agapitus.name: St. Agapitus, Martyr
agapitus.title: Early Roman martyr
agapitus.feast: 18 August (Agapitus of Palestrina) or 7 August (Agapitus the deacon, with Pope St. Sixtus II)
agapitus.summary: The label names a martyr Agapitus but cannot tell us which of several men of that name is meant. He may be the boy martyr of Palestrina, its patron, whose story is largely legend, or the deacon killed in Rome with Pope Sixtus II in 258. Either way he was a young witness to Christ, the age of a Prep student or a servant faithful to his bishop.
life: The label “S. Agapiti M.” gives only the name and “M.” for martyr, and several early martyrs bore this name, which is Greek for “beloved”. The two best known are both from near Rome. St. Agapitus of Palestrina, the ancient Praeneste, was a boy of about fifteen who was put to death for his faith in the third century. The account of his torments is legend, but he was honored at Palestrina from early times, and he is still the town's patron. His feast is 18 August.

St. Agapitus the deacon is on firmer historical ground. He was one of the deacons of Pope St. Sixtus II, and was killed with Felicissimus on 6 August 258, a few hours after the pope, in the persecution of the Emperor Valerian. The early Roman calendars record them, and they were buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus. They are kept today with Sixtus II on 7 August.

Small paper labels written by hand, set on silk in a wooden case, are typical of relics given out from Rome in the 1700s and 1800s, and many of those came from the Roman catacombs. So this may be either of these men, or another martyr of the same name. Only the relic's papers could settle it.
patronage: Palestrina, Italy (if the boy martyr of Praeneste)
why_here: We do not know which Agapitus this is, and it is better to say so. Either way he is a young witness. If he is the boy of Palestrina, he was the age of a Prep student when he died rather than deny Christ. If he is the deacon, he was a servant of the Church who stayed with his bishop to the end. A school for teenagers and a monastery of men vowed to obedience can each find their own reason to ask his prayers.
agapitus.relic: One relic: “S. Agapiti M.” (St. Agapitus, Martyr) in the wooden box with a glass front, beside St. Secundus and, most likely, St. Justina (IMG_4887–4889).

agatha.name: St. Agatha
agatha.title: Virgin and martyr of Catania
agatha.summary: Agatha was martyred at Catania in Sicily around 251 and is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass, though the story of her tortures is largely legend. She is patron of Catania, of women with diseases of the breast, and against fire and volcanoes. The custom of St. Agatha's bread in the German lands suits the abbey's bakery, and her courage speaks to the Prep's girls.
life: Agatha was martyred at Catania in Sicily, probably in the persecution of the Emperor Decius around 251. That she lived and died for Christ there is not in doubt. She was honored very early, and like St. Lucy of Syracuse she is named in the Roman Canon, the oldest Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass. Her name is Greek for “good”. Her cult spread quickly beyond Sicily. In Rome, Pope St. Gregory the Great rededicated a church to her in the 590s, Sant'Agata dei Goti, which had belonged to the Arian Goths.

The account of her death was written down later, and much of it is legend. It says that she was a young woman of a good family who had vowed herself to God, and that a Roman official named Quintianus wanted her. When she refused him he had her arrested and tortured, and her breasts were cut off. St. Peter is said to have come to her in prison and healed her wounds before she died.

Tradition says that a year after her death Mount Etna erupted, and the people of Catania carried her veil out against the stream of lava, and the lava stopped. Since then she has been the protector of the city against fire and the volcano. Her relics were carried off to Constantinople in the 11th century and brought back to Catania in 1126. They are kept in its cathedral, and every February the city holds one of the largest religious festivals in the world in her honor.

Because of the story of her wounds she is prayed to by women with diseases of the breast, and because of the lava she is called on against fire. In parts of Europe, bread is blessed on her feast and kept in the house as a sign of her protection.
patronage: against fire, volcanic eruptions and earthquakes
women with breast cancer and diseases of the breast
why_here: In the German-speaking lands, where the abbey's roots lie, “St. Agatha's bread” has long been blessed on 5 February and kept at home against fire. That gives her a natural place in a monastery with a working bakery, where the ovens run every week.

She is also a good saint for the girls of the Prep. Agatha was a young woman who was pressed by a powerful man and said no, and kept saying it at great cost. Her story is told in harsh terms, but its point is simple. A young woman's body and her choices belong to her and to God, not to whoever has power over her.
agatha.relic: One relic: “s. Agat. V. M.” (St. Agatha, Virgin and Martyr) on the medallion in the velvet case, with St. Francis of Assisi, St. Anthony of Padua, St. Roch and St. Lucy (IMG_4900).

agnes.name: St. Agnes
agnes.title: Virgin and martyr of Rome
agnes.summary: Agnes was a Roman girl of twelve or thirteen killed for her faith, probably around 304, and buried on the Via Nomentana. Later stories of her trials are legend, but her death is well attested. She is patron of girls and young women and of chastity, and was the age of a seventh or eighth grader at the Prep, a reminder that courage is not only for adults.
life: Agnes was a Roman girl who was put to death for her faith, most likely in the last great persecution under Diocletian around 304, though the date is not sure. St. Ambrose of Milan, writing some seventy years later, says she was twelve or thirteen. Pope St. Damasus wrote verses for her tomb, and the poet Prudentius told her story too. So her death is well attested, even if the details are not.

Those details differ from one account to the next, and the later stories are plainly legend. They say she was beautiful and refused to marry, that she was dragged to a brothel and kept from harm, that the fire set to burn her went out, and that she was finally killed by the sword. What is history is that she was buried on the Via Nomentana, outside the walls of Rome. In the 4th century Constantina, the daughter of the Emperor Constantine, built a basilica beside her tomb, and the church of Sant'Agnese still stands there.

Her name sounds like the Latin agnus, a lamb, and from that came a custom kept to this day. On her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome. Their wool is spun and woven by Benedictine nuns into the pallia, the bands of white wool the pope gives to new archbishops each year on 29 June. She is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and Christians have loved her for seventeen centuries as a girl who was braver than the men who judged her. Her skull is kept in another Roman church, Sant'Agnese in Agone on the Piazza Navona, built where the legend says she was exposed to shame.
why_here: Agnes was the age of a seventh or eighth grader at the Prep. That makes her one of the few saints a twelve-year-old can look at as a peer. She did not wait to grow up before she decided whom she belonged to. For the Prep's girls in particular, she is a reminder that faith and courage are not reserved for adults.

She also has a quiet tie to the Benedictine family. Every pallium an archbishop wears is woven by Benedictine nuns from the wool of her lambs, so each year her feast passes through a monastery's hands on its way to the whole Church.
agnes.relic: Two relics: “Oss. S. Agnet. V. M.” (from the bones of St. Agnes, Virgin and Martyr) on the linen board (IMG_4918, 4919), and “s. Agnet. V. M.” on the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965).

aloysius-gonzaga.name: St. Aloysius Gonzaga
aloysius-gonzaga.title: Jesuit, nurse of the plague-stricken
aloysius-gonzaga.summary: Aloysius Gonzaga gave up his inheritance, over his father's long opposition, to become a Jesuit, and died at twenty-three after nursing the sick in a Roman epidemic in 1591. He is patron of young students (Benedict XIII, 1729) and of Christian youth (Pius XI, 1926). He belongs with the abbey's own monks who nursed the sick in epidemics, and with every Prep student weighing a vocation.
life: Aloysius was born in 1568 at Castiglione, in northern Italy, the eldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione, a branch of the powerful Gonzaga family. His father wanted him to be a soldier and a ruler, and dressed him in a little suit of armor as a small boy. He was sent to serve as a page at the court of the Medici in Florence and later at the Spanish court in Madrid. He disliked the life he saw there.

He made up his mind early to give himself to God. He received his First Communion from St. Charles Borromeo in 1580, and he decided to become a Jesuit. His father fought the decision for years. Only in 1585, at seventeen, was Aloysius allowed to give up his inheritance to his younger brother and enter the Jesuit novitiate in Rome. His spiritual director there was St. Robert Bellarmine.

He was a strong-willed young man, and his penances as a boy were harsh enough that his superiors had to rein him in. Later pictures often made him look soft and sugary. The real Aloysius was stubborn, and he learned obedience the hard way.

In 1591 an epidemic struck Rome. The Jesuits opened a hospital, and Aloysius begged in the streets for the sick and carried them in on his back. He washed them, fed them and made their beds, though such work disgusted him. He caught the disease himself and died on 21 June 1591, at twenty-three. He was beatified in 1605, only fourteen years after his death, and canonized in 1726. Three years later Pope Benedict XIII named him patron of young students, and in 1926 Pope Pius XI named him patron of Christian youth. In the 20th century he also came to be invoked by people with AIDS and those who care for them.
patronage: people with AIDS and their caregivers
why_here: He is the Church's patron of young students, and a school is full of them. He was a teenager who had to stand up to his own family over his vocation, which is the kind of thing Prep students thinking about their lives may face.

He also died nursing the sick in an epidemic, and St. Bernard Abbey honors monks who did the same. Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick in the yellow fever of 1878. Frater Hubert Carney, a young monk, died in 1918 after nursing others in the influenza. Aloysius belongs in the same company, and he is a fair patron for the monks who care for their old and sick brothers in the infirmary today.
aloysius-gonzaga.relic: Two relics: a sunburst pendant labelled “S. Aloisii Gonz. C.” (St. Aloysius Gonzaga, Confessor; IMG_4871, 4874, 4877, 4882), and “s. Alois. Gon.” on the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965).

alphonsus-liguori.name: St. Alphonsus Liguori
alphonsus-liguori.title: Bishop, founder of the Redemptorists, Doctor of the Church
alphonsus-liguori.summary: Alphonsus Liguori left the law, founded the Redemptorists to preach to the poor around Naples, and wrote moral theology that taught confessors to be gentle and sensible. He is patron of confessors and moral theologians (Pius XII, 1950). Clear about truth and patient with people, he suits the Prep's theology teachers, and his long, painful old age speaks to the monks of the infirmary.
life: Alphonsus was born near Naples in 1696, the son of a noble family. He was a brilliant student who took a doctorate in law at sixteen and became a successful young lawyer. He is said to have left the law after losing an important case through an oversight, and he was ordained a priest in 1726.

He spent his priesthood with the poorest people around Naples, the goatherds and country people whom the city's clergy seldom reached. In 1732 he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, the Redemptorists, to preach missions to them. In 1762 he was made bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti, a small and poor diocese, much against his will, and he served there until illness forced him to resign in 1775.

He wrote a great deal, and it was read for generations. His books on moral theology taught confessors to be gentle and sensible rather than harsh, steering between those who made sin too easy and those who made salvation too hard. His Glories of Mary, his Visits to the Blessed Sacrament and his Way of the Cross were prayed in Catholic homes and parishes all over the world. He also wrote hymns, among them the Italian Christmas carol “Tu scendi dalle stelle”.

His old age was hard. Rheumatism bent his neck so badly that his chin pressed into his chest. In his last years a dispute with the government of Naples split his own congregation, and for a time he was cut off from the part of it the pope recognized. He died in 1787 at ninety, still in that trial. He was beatified in 1816, canonized in 1839 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1871. In 1950 Pope Pius XII made him patron of confessors and moral theologians.
why_here: The monks teach theology at the Prep, and Alphonsus is the patron of those who teach how to live. His whole method was to be clear about the truth and patient with people, which is the balance any teacher of teenagers needs.

He is also a saint of old age. He lived to ninety in pain, unable to do the work he loved, and his last trial was a split in the community he had founded. The abbey's infirmary is full of men who know something of that: long service, then weakness, and the call to keep praying when they can do nothing else. Alphonsus is a good companion for them.
alphonsus-liguori.relic: Two relics: “S. Alph. d. L.” on the large oval of about ten relics in the velvet case (IMG_4894–4899), and “s. Alph. d Li. E.” (bishop) on the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965).

andrew.name: St. Andrew
andrew.title: Apostle, the first called
andrew.summary: Andrew, a Galilean fisherman and the brother of Simon Peter, was the first called of the apostles, and nearly every Gospel story about him shows him bringing someone to Jesus. Tradition says he was crucified at Patras, but the accounts of his death are legend. He is patron of Scotland and of fishermen, and the natural saint to thank for the abbey's growing vocations.
life: Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida in Galilee and the brother of Simon Peter. In John's Gospel he was first a disciple of John the Baptist. When John pointed to Jesus and called him the Lamb of God, Andrew and another disciple followed Jesus and spent the day with him. Then Andrew went at once to find his brother and told him, “We have found the Messiah”, and brought him to Jesus. For this the Eastern churches call him the “First-Called”.

He appears a few more times in the Gospels, and each time he is bringing someone to Jesus. At the feeding of the five thousand it is Andrew who finds the boy with five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:8–9). When some Greeks came asking to see Jesus, Philip went to Andrew, and the two of them brought the request to the Lord (John 12:20–22).

After the Resurrection the record grows thin. Early writers say he preached around the Black Sea, and later tradition says he preached in Greece and was crucified at Patras. The Acts of Andrew, a writing of the 2nd or 3rd century, tells the story of his death at length, but it is legend. The X-shaped cross that bears his name is a later, medieval tradition.

In 357 his relics were taken to Constantinople, and the Church there has claimed him as its founder ever since. After the crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, most of his relics were brought to Amalfi in Italy, where they have been since 1208. His head was kept in Rome for five centuries, and in 1964 Pope Paul VI gave it back to Patras as a gesture toward the Orthodox. Scotland took him as patron through a legend that some of his relics were carried to St Andrews, and his X-shaped cross is on the Scottish flag. Each year on his feast the pope still sends a delegation to the Ecumenical Patriarch in Istanbul.
why_here: Nearly everything the Gospels tell us about Andrew is about bringing someone else to Jesus. He found his brother, he found the boy with the loaves, he brought the Greeks. That is how vocations usually happen. Someone a young man trusts tells him what he has found. St. Bernard's vocations are increasing, which is uncommon among American Benedictine houses, and Andrew is the obvious saint to thank for that and to ask for more.
andrew.relic: One relic: “S. Andreae Ap.” (St. Andrew, Apostle), in a gilt sunburst with St. Martin and one unread label (IMG_4975).

angelo-of-acri.name: St. Angelo of Acri
angelo-of-acri.title: Capuchin friar, preacher to the poor
angelo-of-acri.summary: Angelo of Acri, born to a poor family in Calabria, entered the Capuchin friars three times before he stayed, and spent nearly forty years preaching missions in plain words to farmers and shepherds. Canonized in 2017, he is patron of his hometown, Acri. He is a comfort to anyone discerning a vocation after a false start, and a model for teachers who must make things plain.
life: Angelo was born Luca Antonio Falcone in 1669 at Acri, a small town in Calabria, at the toe of Italy. His family was poor. As a young man he asked to join the Capuchin friars, a strict branch of the Franciscans, and was received, but he left after a short time. He tried again and left again. He came back a third time in 1690 and stayed, taking the name Angelo. He was ordained a priest in 1700.

His first attempts at preaching went badly. A story told of him says that he had prepared his sermons full of learned quotations and fine phrases, that they failed, and that he then resolved to preach only in the plain words of the Gospel. Whether or not the story is true in its details, that became his way. For nearly forty years he preached missions in the towns and villages of Calabria and the kingdom of Naples. He spoke simply, so that farmers and shepherds could follow him, heard confessions for hours, and worked to make peace between families locked in feuds. He also served his province as its superior. Little was written about him outside Calabria in his lifetime, and most of what we know comes from the inquiries made for his beatification.

He died at Acri on 30 October 1739. He was beatified in 1825 by Pope Leo XII and canonized by Pope Francis in 2017, so the label on the abbey's relic, which calls him “B.” (Blessed), is from the long time between.
why_here: Angelo entered religious life three times before he stayed. That is a comfort to anyone discerning a vocation, at the Prep or in the novitiate. A false start is not the end of the road, and stability, which Benedictines vow, can be learned after failing at it.

He is also a good patron for teachers. His gift was not learning, though he had it, but making the Gospel plain to people who had little schooling. Anyone who has stood in front of a class of seventh graders knows how hard and how important that is.
angelo-of-acri.relic: One relic: “B. Angeli ab Acri” in the Gothic gilt reliquary of Franciscan saints, with St. Francis of Assisi and others (IMG_4970–4972), labelled between his beatification in 1825 and 1839.

anne.name: St. Anne
anne.title: Mother of the Virgin Mary
anne.summary: Anne is honored as the mother of the Virgin Mary, though her name and story come from a 2nd-century writing and should be read as pious story, not history. She is patron of mothers, grandparents and miners, and she was loved especially in Germany. She fits the abbey's German roots and the grandparents who help Prep students through school.
life: The Bible does not name Mary's parents. The names Joachim and Anne come from the Protoevangelium of James, a writing of the 2nd century. The Church never took it into Scripture, but it shaped Christian art and prayer for centuries. In it Anne and Joachim grieve for years because they have no child, until an angel tells each of them that Anne will bear a daughter. When Mary is born, Anne gives her to God, and as a small girl Mary is brought to the Temple. None of this can be checked, and it should be read as pious story, not history.

Devotion to Anne began in the East. In the 6th century the Emperor Justinian built a church in her honor in Constantinople. In Jerusalem, a church near the Pool of Bethesda marks the place where tradition says she lived and Mary was born. In the West her cult grew in the late Middle Ages, and in 1584 her feast was extended to the whole Church. Since 1969 she has been kept together with Joachim on 26 July.

She was loved especially in Germany. Düren, in the Rhineland, has claimed a relic of her head since the early 1500s. Many German towns are named for her, and miners took her as their patron. In 1505 a young law student caught in a thunderstorm cried out, “Help, St. Anne, I will become a monk.” He kept his vow. His name was Martin Luther. Other famous shrines to her are Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré in Quebec and Sainte-Anne-d'Auray in Brittany. Relics of her body are claimed in several places, among them Apt in France, but these rest on tradition alone.
A favorite subject in art is Anne teaching the young Mary to read. In 2021 Pope Francis set a World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly near her feast.
why_here: Anne is the saint of families, and especially of grandparents. Many Prep students are helped through school by grandparents, who pray for them, visit, and sometimes pay. She is a good patron for those families, and for parents who have sent a child away to board.

She also fits the abbey's German roots. Devotion to St. Anne ran deep in the Catholic Germany from which St. Bernard's founders came. The old picture of Anne teaching her daughter to read is a fair image of what the monks have tried to do in Cullman since 1892.
anne.relic: One relic: “s. Annae Matr.” (of St. Anne, Mother [of the Virgin]), in the square theca of the velvet case with the tomb of Our Lady, St. Joseph, St. Peter and St. Paul (IMG_4901, 4902).
anne.credit: chanter Angelos Akotandos (1400 - 1457) Details on Google Art Project · Public domain

anselm.name: St. Anselm
anselm.title: Benedictine abbot, archbishop and Doctor of the Church
anselm.summary: Anselm was a Benedictine monk and abbot of Bec who became Archbishop of Canterbury and a Doctor of the Church, known for his motto “faith seeking understanding”. By custom he is a patron of philosophers, theologians and Benedictine study. A monk under the same Rule as St. Bernard's, he also gave the best advice on teaching the young, which is patience and kindness rather than binding them tight.
life: Anselm was born at Aosta in northern Italy in 1033. After quarreling with his father he left home and wandered for some years through France. In 1059 he came to the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy, drawn by its famous teacher Lanfranc, and the next year he became a monk there. In 1063 he succeeded Lanfranc as prior, and in 1078 he was elected abbot.

At Bec he was a teacher of young monks and a thinker of the first rank. His motto was “faith seeking understanding”. He believed first, and then used his reason to understand what he believed. In the Proslogion he set out his famous argument that God is “that than which nothing greater can be thought”, which philosophers still argue about. His biographer Eadmer tells how an abbot once complained to him that the boys of his monastery were beaten day and night and only grew worse. Anselm asked him what would become of a young tree if it were bound tight on every side, and told him to treat the boys with patience and kindness.

In 1093 he was made Archbishop of Canterbury against his will. He stood up to the English kings William II and Henry I over the freedom of the Church to choose and invest its own bishops, and twice he was sent into exile. During the first exile he finished Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo), which asks why our salvation needed the Son of God to become man and die. A settlement with Henry I was finally reached in 1107. Through all of this he kept writing prayers and meditations, copied and read all over medieval Europe, and letters of warm friendship to his monks.
He died at Canterbury on 21 April 1109. He was named a Doctor of the Church in 1720. The Benedictines' international college in Rome, Sant'Anselmo, bears his name.
patronage: Benedictine study and scholarship (the Benedictine college in Rome, Sant'Anselmo, is named for him)
why_here: Anselm was a Benedictine monk and abbot, living under the same Rule as the monks of St. Bernard. He shows what the Rule can produce when prayer and hard thinking go together.

He is also a patron the Prep's teachers could hardly improve on. “Faith seeking understanding” is a fair summary of a Catholic school's whole purpose, and close to the Prep's own aim of a love of learning and a life of virtue. His advice about the young tree is still the best thing a monk ever said about teaching teenagers. Bind them too tight and they grow crooked. Give them room and care and they grow straight.
anselm.relic: One relic on the linen board: “s. Anselmi Ep. c. d.” (St. Anselm, Bishop, Confessor, Doctor; IMG_4925).

anthony-of-padua.name: St. Anthony of Padua
anthony-of-padua.title: Franciscan preacher, Doctor of the Church
anthony-of-padua.summary: Anthony of Padua, born in Lisbon, became a Franciscan and a famous preacher in Italy and France, and died near Padua in 1231, though many stories told of him are legend. He is best known as patron of lost things and of the poor, through the alms called St. Anthony's Bread. That fits a monastery with a bakery, and boarders who lose keys, phones and their way.
life: He was born Fernando in Lisbon, Portugal, around 1195, to a well-off family. At about fifteen he joined the Augustinian canons, and he studied Scripture deeply at their house in Coimbra. In 1220 the bodies of five Franciscan friars martyred in Morocco were brought to Coimbra. Fernando was so moved that he joined the Franciscans, took the name Anthony, and set out for Africa hoping to die for Christ himself.

Illness drove him back almost as soon as he arrived, and on the voyage home his ship was blown off course and landed in Sicily. He made his way to the friars' great meeting at Assisi in 1221 and was sent to a small hermitage, where nobody knew how learned he was. At an ordination at Forlì the appointed preacher failed to come, and Anthony was told to say something. His sermon astonished everyone. From then on he preached, and St. Francis wrote to him allowing him to teach theology to the friars, as long as study did not put out the spirit of prayer.

He spent his last years preaching to huge crowds in northern Italy and southern France. Many stories are told of him, such as his sermon to the fish at Rimini when the people would not listen. These are legends. He died near Padua on 13 June 1231, about thirty-six years old, and was canonized less than a year later. In 1946 Pope Pius XII named him a Doctor of the Church.

He is best known today as the finder of lost things. The custom grew from a story that a novice who stole his book of psalms was frightened into bringing it back. Alms given to the poor in thanks for his help are called “St. Anthony's Bread”. The familiar picture of him holding the Child Jesus also comes from a later legend.
why_here: The abbey has a working bakery, and Anthony's name is tied to bread. “St. Anthony's Bread” has meant gifts to the hungry for well over a century. A monastery that bakes bread for sale is a natural place to remember that bread is also for giving away.

He is a saint for the Prep as well. Boarders lose things, from keys and phones to their way. Anthony is the saint people ask without embarrassment. And the letter in which St. Francis let him teach, on the condition that study not smother prayer, is good counsel for any school run by monks.
anthony-of-padua.relic: Several: “s. Antonii Pad.” on the medallion in the velvet case (IMG_4900) and on the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965); “Cin. S. Ant. Pat. C.” (ashes of St. Anthony of Padua, Confessor) on the linen board (IMG_4919–4921); and an unnamed medal marked “RELIC” showing a friar with the Child Jesus, likely St. Anthony (IMG_4983, 4984).

augustine.name: St. Augustine of Hippo
augustine.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
augustine.summary: Augustine of Hippo was a brilliant, restless teacher of rhetoric who went a long way wrong before his conversion in 386, helped by his mother Monica's prayers. As bishop of Hippo he wrote the Confessions and The City of God. He is patron of theologians and printers, the name saint of the abbey's webmaster, and a hope for parents worried about a teenager far from home.
life: Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His father was a pagan who was baptized late in life. His mother was St. Monica, a Christian who prayed for him for many years. He was a gifted student and went on to teach rhetoric, the art of public speaking, first in Africa and then in Rome and Milan. He wanted success and got it.

His search for the truth took a long road. At nineteen a book by Cicero turned him toward philosophy. For about nine years he followed the Manichees, a sect that taught that the world was a battle between good and evil powers. For many years he lived with a woman he did not marry, and she bore him a son, Adeodatus.

In Milan he heard the preaching of St. Ambrose, and his doubts began to fall away. In 386, he tells us, he was sitting in a garden in deep distress when he heard a child's voice say, “Take and read.” He opened St. Paul's letters at random, read a passage about putting on Christ, and his struggle ended. He was baptized by Ambrose at Easter 387, together with his son. His mother died soon after, at Ostia, on the way home to Africa.

Back in Africa he lived in a small community of men given to prayer and study. In 391 the people of Hippo pressed him into the priesthood, and a few years later he became their bishop. He served there for more than thirty years. He preached constantly, argued against the errors of his time, and wrote the Confessions, the story of his conversion told as a prayer, and The City of God, written after the sack of Rome in 410. His writing has shaped Western Christianity ever since. He also wrote a short rule for religious communities that many orders still follow. He died on 28 August 430, while the Vandals were besieging his city.
why_here: He is the name saint of Br. Augustine, the abbey's webmaster, who asked for these pages. His relic is fittingly here.

He is also a saint for the Prep's families. Augustine was a brilliant, restless young man who went a long way wrong before he came right, and his mother never stopped praying for him. Parents who send a teenager away to school know something of Monica's worry. And Augustine's most famous line, “our heart is restless until it rests in you”, is a fair description of what students are really looking for, whether they know it yet or not.
augustine.relic: One relic on the linen board: “Oss. S. Aug. Doct.” (from the bones of St. Augustine, Doctor; IMG_4953, 4954).

beatrice-deste.name: Bl. Beatrice I and Bl. Beatrice II d'Este
beatrice-deste.title: Benedictine nuns of the house of Este
beatrice-deste.summary: Bl. Beatrice I and Bl. Beatrice II d'Este, an aunt and her niece of the noble house of Este, left the court to become Benedictine nuns. Each founded a convent, Beatrice I on Monte Gemola and Beatrice II in Ferrara after her betrothed died in battle. They have no widely recognized patronage, but they kept the same Rule the monks of St. Bernard keep today.
life: The Este were one of the great noble families of northern Italy. They took their name from the town of Este, below the Euganean Hills near Padua, and later ruled Ferrara and then Modena. Two daughters of this house, an aunt and her niece, both named Beatrice, left the life of the court to become Benedictine nuns. Both are honored as Blessed. What we know of them comes from short medieval lives and from the long memory of the convents they founded, so the outline is firmer than the details.

Beatrice I was a daughter of Azzo VI, lord of Este. She grew up at the family's castle and, as a young woman, refused the marriage her family could have arranged. She took the veil among Benedictine nuns and then founded a small community of her own on Monte Gemola, a quiet hill in the Euganean range. There she lived a plain life of prayer and work with a few companions, and there she died young, in 1226, probably in her early thirties. Her cult was confirmed by Pope Clement XIII in 1763.

Beatrice II was the daughter of Beatrice I's brother, Azzo VII. Her family promised her in marriage to a nobleman, Galeazzo Manfredi. He died of wounds received in battle before the wedding could take place. Beatrice did not look for another match. She entered religious life and, with her father's help, founded the convent of Sant'Antonio in Polesine in Ferrara, where she lived under the Rule of St. Benedict until her death on 18 January 1262. Benedictine nuns still live there. Her cult was confirmed by Pope Clement XIV in 1774.

Neither woman did anything the world would call great. They prayed, they worked, they kept the Rule, and they each left behind a house where others could do the same. The labels in the abbey's reliquary, "B. Beat. I. Est." and "B. Beat. II. Est.", still give them the title Blessed, which is the title they hold today.
why_here: These two are the only Benedictine nuns in the abbey's reliquary, and they lived the same Rule the monks of St. Bernard keep today. Both chose a hidden life of stability over the position their family could give them. Beatrice II made that choice after a loss that might have broken her, and she built something lasting out of it.

For the Prep's young women, many of them living away from home, these two show that a strong and free choice about one's life can be made young. For the monks, they are a reminder that a monastery is founded and kept alive by ordinary faithful days more than by famous deeds. Their prayers suit anyone who has had a plan collapse and must decide what to build next.
beatrice-deste.relic: Two relics on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), labelled "B. Beat. I. Est." and "B. Beat. II. Est."

benedict.name: St. Benedict of Nursia
benedict.title: Abbot, father of Western monks
benedict.feast: 11 July (21 March in the monastic calendar)
benedict.summary: St. Benedict of Nursia, known to us mainly through the Dialogues of St. Gregory the Great, lived as a hermit at Subiaco and founded Monte Cassino, where he wrote the Rule that most Western monasteries came to follow. He is patron of Europe and of a good death. Every day at St. Bernard Abbey, from the Office to the bakery, is shaped by his Rule.
life: Almost everything we know of Benedict's life comes from one book, the second book of the Dialogues of Pope St. Gregory the Great, written about fifty years after Benedict's death. Gregory names the monks who told him the stories, but he wrote to build up faith, not as a modern historian, and his account is full of wonders. The life below follows Gregory. The plain outline is likely enough. The miracles are best read as the way his first disciples remembered him.

Benedict was born at Nursia (Norcia) in the hills of Umbria, of a free and well-to-do family. Tradition holds that St. Scholastica was his twin sister. He was sent to Rome to study, but the loose life of the city drove him out. He went to Subiaco, east of Rome, and lived for about three years as a hermit in a cave, fed by a monk named Romanus who let down bread on a rope. His name spread, and a community of monks at Vicovaro asked him to be their abbot. His strictness soon wearied them, and Gregory says they put poison in his wine. When Benedict made the sign of the cross over the cup, it shattered. He left them, and at Subiaco he founded twelve small monasteries for the many who came to him.

About 529 he moved south to Monte Cassino, a height above the road from Rome to Naples, where he pulled down an old pagan shrine and built a monastery. There he wrote his Rule. He calls it "a little rule for beginners". Its seventy-three short chapters lay out a whole life. The monks pray the Divine Office together at set hours, which Benedict calls the Work of God. They work with their hands, read Scripture slowly, and live under an abbot who stands in the place of Christ but must answer to God for every soul. The monk promises stability, obedience and conversatio morum, a lifelong turning of his ways toward God. The Rule is strict, but it makes room for the young, the old, the sick and the weak, and it asks the abbot to temper everything so that the strong have something to strive for and the weak are not driven away. The phrase ora et labora, "pray and work", is a later summary of the Rule, not words from it.

Gregory says that Benedict met his sister Scholastica once a year near Monte Cassino, and that on their last visit a storm she had prayed for kept him with her through the night, talking of heaven. She died three days later. In 547, or soon after, Benedict had his grave opened. Six days later, Gregory writes, he had himself carried into the chapel, received the Body and Blood of the Lord, and died standing, his arms raised in prayer and held up by his monks. That death is the reason he is invoked for a good death.

The Rule outlived its author. Monte Cassino was destroyed by the Lombards, by Saracens, and in 1944 by Allied bombing, and was rebuilt each time. Both Monte Cassino and the French abbey of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire) claim his bones. By the 9th century his Rule had become the rule of most monasteries in the West, and the monks who lived it kept learning, farming and the liturgy alive across Europe for centuries. For that reason Pope St. Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.
patronage: monks, nuns and all who live under his Rule
against temptation and evil (especially through the St. Benedict medal)
why_here: Every day at St. Bernard Abbey is shaped by Benedict's Rule. It sets the hours of Matins, Vespers and Compline, the work in the bakery, the farm and the Grotto, the care of the guests and of the old monks in the infirmary, and the vows each monk makes. Benedict is the father of this house in the plainest sense. When the monks ask his prayers they ask for faithfulness to the life he wrote down. Br. Benedict, the head baker and oblate director, bears his name, and the oblates who share the life from outside the cloister follow his Rule too.

For the Prep, Benedict is a patron of schoolchildren in some places, and his Rule is about learning to live with others, to listen (its first word is "Listen"), and to keep at a good thing for a long time. Boarders far from home live a little like his monks. He is also the one to ask for a good death, for the monks in the infirmary and those buried in the abbey cemetery.
benedict.relic: Two relics: a cross-shaped gold reliquary labelled "[S.] Benedicti Abb." (IMG_4916), and a theca on the large linen board labelled "S. Benedicti Ab. C." (of St. Benedict, Abbot and Confessor).

bernadette.name: St. Bernadette Soubirous
bernadette.title: Visionary of Lourdes, Sister of Charity of Nevers
bernadette.summary: St. Bernadette Soubirous was a poor, sickly girl of Lourdes who said that in 1858 a lady appeared to her eighteen times at the grotto of Massabielle, a private revelation the Church has approved. She later became a Sister of Charity at Nevers and is a patron of the sick and the poor. She is a natural friend to the monks who keep the Ave Maria Grotto.
life: Bernadette Soubirous was born in Lourdes, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, on 7 January 1844, the eldest child of a miller. The family lost its mill and fell into poverty, and by 1857 they were living in a damp former jail cell called the cachot. Bernadette suffered from asthma, had little schooling and spoke the local dialect rather than French. At fourteen she had not yet made her First Communion because she could not learn the catechism.

On 11 February 1858, while gathering firewood by the river Gave, she saw at the mouth of a grotto called Massabielle a young lady dressed in white with a blue sash. Over the next months she said the lady appeared to her eighteen times. The lady asked for prayer and penance for sinners and for a chapel to be built, and told Bernadette to drink from a spring. Bernadette dug in the mud of the grotto, and a spring began to flow there. On 25 March the lady said, "I am the Immaculate Conception", words Bernadette did not understand but repeated to the parish priest. The town was divided. Bernadette was questioned by the police and the clergy many times. She never changed her account and never took money or gifts.

In 1862 the bishop of Tarbes declared that the faithful could believe the apparitions were real. The Church's approval of Lourdes, like that of Fatima, is approval of a private revelation, which no one is bound to believe. Pilgrims began to come in great numbers, and many cures have been claimed at the spring. The Church has recognized only a few of them as miraculous, after long medical study.

Bernadette wanted to get away from the crowds. In 1866 she joined the Sisters of Charity of Nevers and took the name Marie-Bernard. She never saw Lourdes again. She worked as an assistant in the infirmary and then in the sacristy, and she was often ill herself. When a superior treated her coldly, she bore it without complaint. She said that her task was to be ill, and that the Blessed Virgin had used her like a broom and then put her back in her corner. She died at Nevers on 16 April 1879, aged 35, of tuberculosis of the bone. She was canonized by Pius XI in 1933. Her body, found well preserved when it was exhumed, lies in a glass shrine at Nevers.
why_here: Lourdes is a grotto, and the abbey's best-known work is a grotto too. Br. Joseph Zoettl built the Ave Maria Grotto out of stone, shells, glass and scrap, a poor man's work in praise of Our Lady, and it has drawn pilgrims to Cullman since 1934. Bernadette, a poor girl at a cave by a river, is a natural friend to that work and to the monks who keep it.

She also fits the Prep. She was behind in school, unsure of herself, and questioned by people who thought her foolish, yet she told the truth plainly and would not be bought. For a student who feels slow or out of place, or who is laughed at for believing, she is a good companion. Her years in the infirmary make her a friend of the abbey's sick monks too.
bernadette.relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "S. M. Bernardae" (of St. Maria Bernarda, her name as a sister).

bernard-of-clairvaux.name: St. Bernard of Clairvaux
bernard-of-clairvaux.title: Abbot and Doctor of the Church, patron of this abbey
bernard-of-clairvaux.summary: St. Bernard of Clairvaux brought some thirty relatives and friends into the poor monastery of Cîteaux, was abbot of Clairvaux for thirty-eight years, and spread the Cistercians across Europe. A Doctor of the Church, he is best known for his writing on the love of God and on Our Lady, and he is a patron of beekeepers. He is the patron of this abbey and its school.
life: Bernard was born in 1090 at Fontaines, near Dijon in Burgundy, one of seven children of a knight. His mother, Aleth, was devout and he was close to her, and her death when he was a young man moved him deeply. He was clever, well read and good company, and could have had a career in the world or in the Church. Instead, about 1112 or 1113, he knocked at the gate of Cîteaux, a new and very poor monastery that wanted to keep the Rule of St. Benedict to the letter. He did not come alone. He brought some thirty relatives and friends with him, among them several of his brothers, whom he had talked into the life one by one.

Cîteaux had been close to dying out. After Bernard's arrival it grew so fast that within three years it was sending out monks to found new houses. In 1115 Bernard, then about twenty-five, was sent with twelve monks to a wild valley in Champagne. They called it Clairvaux, the clear valley. The first years were hard, with poor food and fierce fasting, and Bernard later admitted he had been too severe with himself and with others. He was abbot of Clairvaux for thirty-eight years. From it some sixty-eight new monasteries were founded in his lifetime, and through him the Cistercians, the reformed Benedictines of Cîteaux, spread across Europe.

Bernard never wanted to leave his cloister, but popes, kings and bishops kept calling him out of it. When two men were elected pope in 1130, he travelled for years to win the Church over to Innocent II, and the schism ended in 1138. One of his own monks became Pope Eugene III, and Bernard wrote him a book, On Consideration, warning him not to let business crowd out prayer. He opposed the teaching of Peter Abelard and had it condemned at Sens in 1141. In 1146, at the pope's request, he preached the Second Crusade at Vézelay. The crusade ended in disaster, and Bernard took the blame bitterly. When a monk preached that the crusaders should first kill the Jews of the Rhineland, Bernard went to Germany himself, stopped him and defended the Jews. Some of his actions, and his harshness in argument, are hard to admire today. He was a great man, and also a difficult one.

He was above all a writer and preacher on the love of God. In On Loving God he says that the reason for loving God is God himself, and the measure is to love without measure. His eighty-six sermons on the Song of Songs, given to his monks over eighteen years, read the love poem as the story of God and the soul. He wrote and preached on Our Lady with warmth, and his homily on the Annunciation gave the Church the words "Look to the star, call upon Mary." The famous prayer called the Memorare is often credited to him, but in its present form it comes from a later time. Dante, in the last cantos of the Paradiso, chose Bernard to lead him to the vision of God and put in his mouth the great prayer to the Virgin.

Bernard died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153. He was canonized in 1174, only twenty-one years later, and Pope Pius VIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1830. He is called the "Mellifluous Doctor", the teacher whose words flow like honey, and in 1953 Pope Pius XII wrote an encyclical on him with that title, Doctor Mellifluus. He is often shown with a beehive, and for that reason he became the patron of beekeepers and of candle makers, who work with wax. Images of him often show the white Cistercian habit, a book, and Our Lady.
patronage: St. Bernard Abbey and St. Bernard Preparatory School
why_here: Bernard is the patron of this abbey and its school, and his name is on everything here, from the Prep to the Clairvaux Society that supports both. He was a Benedictine by Rule, one who wanted to live it more simply and fully, and he trained a great many young men to do the same. That makes him a fitting patron for a community whose vocations are increasing. His life also shows the strain between the cloister and the work outside it, a strain the monks know when they teach, coach, run a Retreat Center and keep the Grotto.

For the Prep, he is the young man who chose his path at twenty-two and brought his friends with him, and a writer whose Latin is still read. His honey and wax link him to the monks' candle making. He also knew failure, after the Second Crusade, and kept going. The abbey keeps four relics of him, as many as of any saint in the reliquary.
bernard-of-clairvaux.relic: Four relics: a round gold reliquary ringed with rhinestones, "S. Bernardi Ab. D." (IMG_4885); a gilt Gothic tabernacle, "S. Bernardi" (4976); a gilt theca with open loops, "S. Bern. A. D." (4991); and one label on the oval of fifteen relics (4965).

blaise.name: St. Blaise
blaise.title: Bishop and martyr
blaise.summary: St. Blaise is said to have been bishop of Sebaste in Armenia and a martyr about 316, but little beyond his name, his town and his death is certain. A legend that he healed a boy choking on a fish bone made him the patron against ailments of the throat and of wool combers. Each 3 February the monks give the Prep his blessing of throats.
life: St. Blaise is one of the most loved saints of the Middle Ages and one of the least known to history. He is said to have been bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, now Sivas in Turkey, and to have been martyred about 316 under the Emperor Licinius, who persecuted Christians in the East after Constantine had made peace with the Church in the West. Almost nothing beyond his name, his town and his death is certain. His written Acts are late and full of legend.

The earliest firm trace of his cult is medical. Aëtius of Amida, a Greek physician of the 6th century, told doctors treating a patient with something stuck in the throat to call on "Blaise, martyr and servant of Christ". The legend explains why. As Blaise was being led to prison, a mother brought him her son, who was choking to death on a fish bone. Blaise prayed over the boy and he was healed.

Other stories filled out his life. He is said to have fled persecution and lived in a cave, where wild animals came to him to be healed. A poor woman's pig was carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf brought it back. When he was in prison, the woman brought him food and candles. The legend says his flesh was torn with iron combs, the kind used to card wool, before he was beheaded. From that story he became the patron of wool combers.

His cult spread widely in the East and the West. He was counted among the Fourteen Holy Helpers, saints invoked together in the Rhineland and Bavaria for help in particular troubles. Dubrovnik on the Adriatic took him as its patron. On his feast, priests still bless throats with two crossed candles, praying that through his intercession the person may be kept from ailments of the throat and from every other illness.
why_here: The blessing of throats on 3 February is one of the few rites of the year that reaches every student in a Catholic school, and at the Prep it is the monks who give it. A choir monk sings the Office several times a day, and teachers, choirmasters and coaches use their voices all day long. Blaise is a practical patron for all of them.

He was also one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, a devotion of the German and Bavarian Catholics from whom the abbey and Cullman both descend. His legends are honest about what they are, stories of care for a frightened mother, a choking child, a poor woman's pig, and the animals of the wild. A monastery with a cattle farm and chickens can take that last one in good humor.
blaise.relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled for St. Blaise.

bonaventure.name: St. Bonaventure
bonaventure.title: Franciscan, cardinal, the Seraphic Doctor
bonaventure.summary: St. Bonaventure was a Franciscan friar, a master of theology at Paris alongside St. Thomas Aquinas, and for seventeen years the minister general who held a divided order together. A Doctor of the Church called the Seraphic Doctor, he is a patron of theologians and of his hometown, Bagnoregio. He is a scholar's saint for the Prep and a model of patient governance for the abbey.
life: Bonaventure was born Giovanni di Fidanza at Bagnoregio, a hill town near Viterbo, about 1217 (some say 1221). His father was a physician. Later he wrote that as a small boy he had been cured of a grave illness through the prayers of St. Francis, and the story that Francis himself greeted him with "O buona ventura", "Oh, good fortune", is a legend. He went to Paris to study and there joined the Franciscan friars, about 1243. He studied under Alexander of Hales and became a master of theology. He and St. Thomas Aquinas were received as masters at the university at the same time, in 1257, after a long quarrel over whether the begging friars should teach there at all.

In 1257 he was elected minister general of the Franciscans. The order was large and divided. Some friars wanted to keep Francis's poverty to the letter, others had settled into houses and schools, and a radical party was spreading wild prophecies about the end of the age. Bonaventure led them for seventeen years. He wrote constitutions for the order, visited its houses on foot, and steered a middle path that kept both poverty and learning. In 1263 he finished the Major Life of St. Francis, which the order made its official life, and soon after the earlier lives were ordered destroyed. Historians still argue about that decision.

He was a theologian of the heart as well as the head. In 1259, on Mount La Verna, where Francis had received the stigmata, he wrote The Journey of the Mind into God, a short book that leads the reader from the things of the world, through the soul, to God, and ends in love rather than knowledge. His Breviloquium is a compact summary of the faith. He taught that all learning should lead to holiness.

Pope Gregory X made him cardinal-bishop of Albano in 1273. A story says that the messengers who brought the cardinal's hat found him washing dishes and asked them to hang it on a tree until he had finished. He helped prepare the Second Council of Lyon, which tried to reunite the Greek and Latin churches, and died during it on 15 July 1274. He was canonized in 1482 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1588, with the title "Seraphic Doctor".
why_here: Bonaventure held a divided community together for seventeen years without forcing it into one shape, by patience, visits and clear rules. Any abbot and his council could ask his prayers for that kind of steady governance. He also never set study against prayer, which is the Benedictine instinct too.

For the Prep he is a scholar's saint. He was a colleague, and sometimes a rival, of St. Thomas Aquinas, the patron of Br. Thomas, the abbey's librarian, and the two of them stand together as the great teachers of the 13th century. Theology and Latin teachers at the Prep teach in the tradition he helped build. The dish-washing story, legend though it is, is a fair lesson for students who are good at their books.
bonaventure.relic: One relic on the large oval of fifteen relics in a pewter-coloured frame (IMG_4965), labelled for St. Bonaventure.

camillus-de-lellis.name: St. Camillus de Lellis
camillus-de-lellis.title: Founder of the Ministers of the Sick
camillus-de-lellis.feast: 14 July (18 July in the United States)
camillus-de-lellis.summary: St. Camillus de Lellis was a soldier and gambler who, after his conversion, founded the Ministers of the Sick, men who vowed to nurse the sick even at the risk of their own lives. Leo XIII named him patron of the sick and of hospitals, and Pius XI added nurses. The abbey honors monks who nursed the sick in epidemics, and he suits its infirmary.
life: Camillus was born in 1550 at Bucchianico in the Abruzzi, in southern Italy. His mother was nearly sixty and died when he was a boy. His father was a soldier, often away, and Camillus grew up with little guidance. He was very tall, with a quick temper and a passion for cards and dice. As a young man he went soldiering as a mercenary, fought for Venice against the Turks, and gambled away all he had. In 1574 he was in Naples with nothing left, he is said to have lost even his shirt, and he took work as a laborer on a building for the Capuchin friars at Manfredonia.

There, in February 1575, after a talk with one of the friars, he was converted. He tried twice to become a Capuchin, but each time a sore on his leg that would not heal forced him to leave. The wound took him to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, first as a patient and then as a servant, and in time he became its master of the house. He was shocked by what he saw. The sick were left dirty, unfed and alone, and hired attendants were often cruel. He gathered a few men who would nurse the sick for the love of God, as a mother nurses her only child.

With St. Philip Neri as his confessor, he studied for the priesthood in his thirties, alongside boys, and was ordained in 1584. His company, the Ministers of the Sick, was approved in 1586. The members wore a large red cross on their habits and added a fourth vow to serve the sick even at the risk of their own lives. They nursed in the hospitals of Rome and Naples, on the ships of the plague-stricken, and on the battlefields of Hungary and Croatia, and many of them died of the diseases they nursed.

Camillus himself was ill for much of his life, with the leg wound, a rupture and other pains, yet he would still go from bed to bed in the night. He resigned as superior general in 1607 and died in Rome on 14 July 1614. He was canonized in 1746. Pope Leo XIII named him, with St. John of God, patron of the sick and of hospitals in 1886, and Pius XI added nurses in 1930.
why_here: The abbey honors monks who did exactly what Camillus asked of his men. Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick in the yellow fever of 1878. Frater Hubert Carney died in 1918 nursing others in the influenza. Fr. Urban Tracy served lepers. Camillus would have recognized them. His prayers are fitting for the brothers who now care for the old and sick monks in the abbey infirmary, and for the monks who are patients there.

He is also a saint for young people who start badly. He was a gambler and a brawler in his twenties and found his life's work only after he had wrecked his plans. A Prep student who has made a mess of things, or who is thinking about nursing or medicine, could do worse than ask his help.
camillus-de-lellis.relic: Two relics: a sunburst stand and pendant (IMG_4872, 4875, 4876, 4883), and a theca on the large linen board labelled for St. Camillus de Lellis.

catherine-laboure.name: St. Catherine Labouré
catherine-laboure.title: Daughter of Charity, visionary of the Miraculous Medal
catherine-laboure.summary: St. Catherine Labouré was a farmer's daughter who became a Daughter of Charity and said that in 1830 Our Lady asked her to have the Miraculous Medal made. She kept that secret for decades while caring for old men, minding a door and keeping poultry. A patron of the elderly by tradition, she shows the monks that such humble work can be the whole of a holy life.
life: Zoé Labouré was born in 1806 at Fain-lès-Moutiers in Burgundy, one of the many children of a farmer. Her mother died when she was nine, and the story is told that she took a statue of Our Lady in her arms and asked her to be her mother now. From about twelve she ran her father's house and farm, with its kitchen, its laborers and its dovecote. She did not learn to read and write until much later. Her father opposed her wish to be a nun, but at twenty-four she was received into the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul and took the name Catherine.

In 1830, as a novice in the convent in the Rue du Bac in Paris, she said she was woken one July night by a child who led her to the chapel, where Our Lady sat and spoke with her for hours. On 27 November she said she saw Mary standing on a globe with rays of light from her hands, framed by the words "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to you", and then the reverse, an M with a cross and two hearts. She was told to have a medal made. Her confessor, Fr. Aladel, was slow to believe her, but in 1832, with the archbishop's leave, the first medals were struck. Paris was suffering an outbreak of cholera, and the medal spread so fast and with so many reported cures that people began calling it the Miraculous Medal.
These apparitions are a private revelation, which no one is bound to believe. The medal itself is a sacramental, a sign that leads to prayer, not a charm.

Catherine asked that her name be kept secret, and it was. For about forty-five years she worked at a hospice for old men at Reuilly, outside Paris. She minded the door, did the laundry, cooked, and kept the poultry, and the other sisters thought her plain and rather dull. Only months before her death on 31 December 1876 did she tell her superior that she was the sister of the medal. She was canonized by Pius XII in 1947. Her body rests in the chapel of the Rue du Bac.
patronage: those who wear the Miraculous Medal
why_here: Catherine spent most of her life caring for old men, answering a door and keeping chickens, and no one knew who she was. A monastery with an infirmary for its old and sick monks, guest masters at the door, and some forty chickens on its farm has plenty of that kind of work. She shows that it can be the whole of a holy life.

She also grew up running a farmhouse at twelve after her mother's death and could not read until she was grown. For a Prep student who carries more at home than classmates know, or who came late to learning, she is a quiet ally. Many families at the school will have a Miraculous Medal in a drawer, and her story gives them its history.
catherine-laboure.relic: Two relics: one in a gilt pendant on the large linen board shared with St. Philip Neri and St. John Vianney, and one in a gilt crown-of-thorns pendant in the white linen case (IMG_4981).

catherine-of-siena.name: St. Catherine of Siena
catherine-of-siena.title: Dominican tertiary, Doctor of the Church
catherine-of-siena.summary: St. Catherine of Siena, a wool dyer's daughter with little schooling, nursed the sick through the plague and dictated hundreds of letters, urging Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. A Doctor of the Church, she is patron of Italy and co-patron of Europe. She shows the Prep's students that a young person can speak to those in charge with courage and charity.
life: Caterina Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, the twenty-fourth child of a wool dyer, Jacopo, and his wife Lapa. Her twin sister died as a baby. From childhood she was drawn to prayer. When her family began to arrange a marriage for her in her teens, she cut off her hair, and they punished her by making her the household servant. She did the work without complaint, and her father in the end let her be. At about sixteen she was received among the Mantellate, Dominican lay women who wore the habit but lived in their own homes.

For three years she lived almost in silence in a small room in her father's house. Then she came out to serve. She nursed the sick in Siena's hospitals, including those whose diseases others shunned, and stayed with the dying during the plague of 1374. She visited prisoners, and is said to have walked with a young man condemned to death to the scaffold, holding his head as he died. A circle of friends, priests, nobles and poor women, gathered round her and called her "Mamma".

She learned to read as a young woman and to write only late in her short life, but she dictated hundreds of letters to popes, kings, captains and ordinary people. About 380 survive. In them she wrote bluntly to Pope Gregory XI, then living at Avignon in France, and urged him to come back to Rome and to reform the Church. She went to Avignon in 1376 to tell him in person. He returned to Rome in 1377. When the Great Schism broke out the next year, she threw her strength behind Pope Urban VI. Her book, The Dialogue, is a conversation between the soul and God about truth, love and the Church.

Worn out by fasting and labor, she died in Rome on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. She was canonized in 1461. Pius XII named her, with St. Francis, patron of Italy in 1939. In 1970 Paul VI made her one of the first two women Doctors of the Church, with St. Teresa of Ávila, and in 1999 John Paul II named her a co-patron of Europe.
why_here: Catherine had no title, no office and little schooling, and she still told a pope to his face what he needed to hear. She shows the Prep's students, girls especially, that a young person can speak with courage and charity to those in charge, and that conviction is worth more when it is joined to service. She did her first great work in her teens and early twenties.

For the monks she is a reminder that prayer and action are not rivals. She lived three years in near silence and then nursed plague victims and wrote to princes. She also loved the Church enough to criticize it honestly and stay in it, which is a grace every religious community needs.
