catherine-of-siena.relic: One relic on the large oval of fifteen relics in a pewter-coloured frame (IMG_4965), labelled for St. Catherine of Siena.

charbel.name: St. Charbel Makhlouf
charbel.title: Maronite monk and hermit
charbel.summary: St. Charbel Makhlouf was a Lebanese Maronite monk who spent sixteen years in the monastery of Annaya and twenty-three as a hermit above it, praying, working the land and keeping silence. Many healings have been reported since his death, and he is a patron of Lebanon and of the sick. He is a brother across rites to monks who vow stability and work the abbey's land.
life: Youssef Makhlouf was born in 1828 at Bekaa Kafra, a high mountain village in northern Lebanon. His father, a mule driver, died when he was three, and an uncle raised him. As a boy he tended the family's cow and was known for praying in a cave near the village. Two of his mother's brothers were hermits, and he visited them often. At twenty-three he left home without telling his family and entered the Lebanese Maronite Order, at the monastery of Our Lady of Mayfouk. He took the name Charbel, after an early martyr of Edessa.

The Maronites are Eastern Catholics, in full communion with Rome, whose liturgy is in Syriac and Arabic. Charbel studied theology at the monastery of Kfifan, where one of his teachers was St. Nimatullah Kassab Al-Hardini, also a monk and now also a saint. He was ordained priest in 1859 and sent to the monastery of St. Maron at Annaya. For sixteen years he lived there as an ordinary monk, praying the Office, working in the fields and vineyards, and keeping silence and obedience so exactly that others noticed.

In 1875 he was allowed to move to the hermitage of Sts. Peter and Paul, on the hill above Annaya. He lived there for twenty-three years under a strict rule, eating once a day, sleeping little on a mat of leaves, working the hermitage land and spending long hours before the Blessed Sacrament. In December 1898 he suffered a stroke while saying Mass, and he died on Christmas Eve.

After his burial, people reported a bright light over his grave. When the tomb was opened some months later, the body was found to be intact and seeping a fluid like sweat and blood, and many reports of healing followed. These reports, and the state of the body, drew pilgrims from all over Lebanon and beyond. The Church did not rest his cause on the body, but on his life and on cures it examined. Paul VI beatified him at the close of the Second Vatican Council in 1965 and canonized him in 1977.
why_here: Charbel was a monk who spent his whole life within a few miles of one monastery, praying the Office, working the land and keeping silence. Nothing he did would make the news, and that is the point. The monks of St. Bernard make a vow of stability, and many of them work the abbey's farm, garden and grounds. Charbel is a brother to them across the Mediterranean and across rites.

He is also a reminder that the Benedictine West is not the whole of monastic life. The Eastern monks, of whom he is the best known in modern times, keep traditions older than Benedict. Students who come to the Prep from abroad, or from Eastern Catholic families, may find in him a saint of their own.
charbel.relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "S." (Saint) Charbel, so written after his canonization in 1977.

clare.name: St. Clare of Assisi
clare.title: Founder of the Poor Clares
clare.summary: St. Clare of Assisi left her noble family at eighteen to follow St. Francis, who cut off her hair, and she lived over forty years in poverty and prayer at San Damiano. She wrote the first rule for women written by a woman, and Pius XII named her patron of television. The abbey's relic of her is a lock of that hair, the sign of a young person's choice.
life: Chiara Offreduccio was born in Assisi in 1194, into a noble family. As a girl she was known for her prayer and her gifts to the poor. When she was about eighteen she heard Francis of Assisi preach, and met him in secret several times. On the night after Palm Sunday 1212, she slipped out of her family's house by a side door and went to the little chapel of the Porziuncola, where Francis and his brothers met her with torches. Francis cut off her hair as a sign that she now belonged to God, and she put on a rough habit. Her family came to drag her home, but she held to the altar and showed them her shorn head, and they gave up. Within weeks her younger sister Agnes joined her.

After short stays with Benedictine nuns, Clare and her sisters settled at San Damiano, the small church outside Assisi that Francis had rebuilt with his own hands. She lived there for forty-one years and hardly left. The sisters prayed, worked with their hands, and owned nothing. Clare spun thread and sewed altar linens for poor churches even when she was confined to bed. She fought for years for the right of her community to have no property or income at all, and got it as a "privilege of poverty" from the pope. She cared for Francis in his last illness and outlived him by twenty-seven years.

Tradition tells that in 1240, when soldiers of the Emperor Frederick II, many of them Saracens, climbed the walls of San Damiano, Clare, ill as she was, had the Blessed Sacrament carried out before them and prayed, and the soldiers fled. That is why she is often shown holding a monstrance. Another story tells that one Christmas, too sick to go to Mass, she saw and heard it on the wall of her room. For that reason Pius XII named her patron of television.

Clare wrote her own Rule, the first rule for women written by a woman. Pope Innocent IV approved it on 9 August 1253, and she died two days later. She was canonized by Alexander IV in 1255. Her sisters, the Poor Clares, still live in enclosed communities around the world.
why_here: The abbey's relic of Clare is a lock of her hair, and that is the very thing Francis cut off on the night she gave her life to God. It is a relic of a young woman's decision, made at eighteen, against her family's plans. The Prep's students are near that age, many of them already thinking about what their lives are for.

Clare is also a saint of stability. She lived over forty years in one small convent, as the monks vow to live in one monastery. She worked with her hands at spinning and sewing, the kind of work the abbey's tailors still do, and she ran her community firmly and kindly for four decades. Her Rule, like Benedict's, puts poverty and prayer at the center.
clare.relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "Ex capillis", from her hair.

claude-de-la-colombiere.name: St. Claude de la Colombière
claude-de-la-colombiere.title: Jesuit priest, apostle of the Sacred Heart
claude-de-la-colombiere.summary: St. Claude de la Colombière was a French Jesuit who, as confessor to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, judged her visions of the Sacred Heart to be from God and spread that devotion. He was imprisoned and banished from England during the panic of the Popish Plot. He has no formal patronage, but he is a good friend to anyone discerning a vocation that does not feel easy at first.
life: Claude de la Colombière was born in 1641 near Lyon, in southeastern France, into a family of the minor nobility. He was taught by the Jesuits and entered their order at seventeen. Later, in his private notes, he admitted that he had felt a strong natural dislike for the life he chose. He was a gifted man, a fine preacher and writer, and taught rhetoric in Jesuit colleges. In 1674, during his long retreat before final vows, he made a private vow to keep the rules of his order perfectly, a vow he held to for the rest of his life.

In 1675 he was sent as superior to the small Jesuit house at Paray-le-Monial in Burgundy. There he became the confessor of a Visitation nun, Margaret Mary Alacoque, who said she had received visions of Christ showing her his heart and asking that it be honored. Her sisters and superiors doubted her. Claude listened carefully, judged that her experience came from God, and encouraged her. He spread the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus in his own preaching and writing.

In 1676 he was sent to London as preacher to Mary of Modena, the Duchess of York and wife of the future King James II, herself a daughter of the House of Este. At the court of a Protestant country he preached, heard confessions and helped converts back to the Church. In 1678 the panic of the "Popish Plot", a story of a Catholic conspiracy made up by Titus Oates, swept England. Claude was denounced, arrested and held in a damp prison, then banished from England early in 1679.

His lungs never recovered. He returned to France, served as spiritual director to young Jesuits at Lyon, and was sent back to Paray in the hope that the air would help him. He died there on 15 February 1682, at forty-one. His retreat notes and letters were published after his death and are still read, especially his "Act of Confidence in God". He was beatified in 1929 and canonized by John Paul II in 1992.
patronage: devotion to the Sacred Heart (by association, not a formal patronage)
why_here: Claude chose religious life while feeling a strong aversion to it, and he said so honestly. That makes him a good friend for students at the Prep who are discerning their lives, and for young monks in formation, because a vocation does not always feel easy or natural at first. What carried him was trust, which is the theme of his best-known prayer.

He was also a careful listener. He believed a young nun whom others dismissed, after testing what she said. Teachers and monks who hear students' troubles, and priests who hear confessions, can ask for his patient judgment. His prison and exile give him a claim too on the prayers of all who are falsely accused.
claude-de-la-colombiere.relic: One relic on the large linen board, labelled "B. Cl. d. la Colom[bière]", so written between his beatification in 1929 and his canonization in 1992.

columba-marmion.name: Bl. Columba Marmion
columba-marmion.title: Abbot of Maredsous, spiritual writer
columba-marmion.summary: Bl. Columba Marmion was an Irish priest who became a monk of Maredsous in Belgium and later its third abbot. His conferences to his monks, published as books such as Christ, the Life of the Soul, were read in monasteries and seminaries for decades. He has no official patronage, but he is a natural patron for the abbey's novices and for those who form them.
life: Joseph Marmion was born in Dublin on 1 April 1858, to an Irish father and a French mother. He studied for the priesthood at Clonliffe College in Dublin and at the Irish College in Rome, and was ordained in Rome in 1881. On his way home he visited the Benedictine abbey of Maredsous in Belgium and was drawn to it, but his bishop wanted him in Dublin. For five years he served as a curate and then as a professor of philosophy at Clonliffe, and as chaplain to a convent and a women's prison.

In 1886, with his bishop's leave, he entered Maredsous and took the name Columba, after the Irish monk of Iona. It was hard for him. He was nearly thirty, a priest used to his own ways, now a novice among much younger Belgian men, living in French and under a strict German-trained discipline. He persevered and made his vows in 1888. In 1899 he helped found the abbey of Mont César at Louvain, where he taught theology to young monks and became confessor to Cardinal Mercier, the archbishop of Mechelen.

In 1909 he was elected the third abbot of Maredsous. He was a warm, humorous and approachable abbot, a good preacher, and much in demand for retreats. His conferences to his monks, written down and edited by a fellow monk, became books. Christ, the Life of the Soul (1917), Christ in His Mysteries (1919) and Christ, the Ideal of the Monk (1922) were translated into many languages and read in monasteries, seminaries and convents for decades. Their theme is simple. We become sons of God by grace, in Christ, and the whole spiritual life is to live out that adoption.

When the German army occupied Belgium in 1914, he sent his young monks to Ireland, where they could continue their formation in peace, and he made the difficult wartime journey himself to see to them. The war years were full of worry and debt. He died at Maredsous on 30 January 1923, during an influenza epidemic. John Paul II beatified him in 2000.
patronage: spiritual reading and those who teach the faith (by association)
why_here: Marmion was a Benedictine abbot whose life work was teaching his monks, and the abbey's novice master, abbot and teachers do the same work. His books were long the standard reading in American Benedictine houses and seminaries, and the monks of St. Bernard, who ran a seminary here for years, may well have read him in their formation. He is a modern Benedictine for a modern abbey.

He also entered religious life late and found it hard, and he cared about the formation of young monks enough to move them out of a war zone. His prayers suit the abbey's growing number of novices and juniors, and those who form them. His chief theme, that a Christian is a son or daughter of God in Christ, is a good one for teenagers trying to understand who they are.
columba-marmion.relic: A clothing relic, labelled "Ex Indumentis" and "B." (Blessed): in a gilt sunburst (IMG_4891) and in a clear case in the white linen case (IMG_4987), perhaps the same theca photographed twice.

conrad-of-parzham.name: St. Conrad of Parzham
conrad-of-parzham.title: Capuchin brother, porter of Altötting
conrad-of-parzham.summary: St. Conrad of Parzham was a Bavarian farmer who became a Capuchin lay brother and served for forty-one years as porter of the friary at Altötting, receiving pilgrims, the poor and children with patience. By tradition he is a patron of porters and of Altötting's pilgrims. He suits the abbey's guest masters, and he comes from the same Bavaria as Metten Abbey.
life: Johann Birndorfer was born in 1818 at Parzham, a farming hamlet in Lower Bavaria, one of the many children of a prosperous and devout farm family. He lost both his parents in his teens. He stayed on the farm and worked it for years, praying the rosary as he worked, walking long distances to Mass and to shrines, and joining a lay confraternity. In 1849, at thirty-one, he gave away his share of the inheritance and asked to join the Capuchin friars as a lay brother. He took the name Conrad and made his vows in 1852.

He was sent at once to the friary of St. Anne at Altötting, beside the shrine of the Black Madonna, the most visited place of pilgrimage in Bavaria. He was made porter, the brother who answers the door, and he kept that job for forty-one years. Altötting drew huge crowds, and the friary door was busy all day. Pilgrims came to ask for a priest or for directions, the poor came for food, and children came because he gave them bread and sometimes a holy picture. He answered each with patience, a few words of advice, and often a reminder to pray. People later said that he seldom spoke much but never sent anyone away unheard.

His nights were given to prayer. Near the door there was a small room from which he could see the tabernacle in the church, and he spent much of his spare time there. He fasted and slept little, yet was always calm and cheerful. When he was asked about his life he said that the cross was his book.

In April 1894, old and ill, he gave up his post. He died a few days later, on 21 April. Pilgrims and the people of Altötting at once began to treat him as a saint. He was beatified by Pius XI in 1930 and canonized by the same pope in 1934. His body rests in the friary church, which now bears his name.
why_here: St. Benedict tells the porter of a monastery to answer every knock with "Thanks be to God" and to receive each guest as Christ. Conrad lived exactly that for forty-one years. The abbey's guest masters, the monks who run the Retreat Center, and those who meet pilgrims at the Ave Maria Grotto are doing his work. Abbot Brendan was himself a guest master. Conrad is their natural patron.

He was also a Bavarian farm boy, from the same Catholic Bavaria as Metten Abbey, the mother of St. Vincent and so the grandmother of St. Bernard. Cullman was settled by German immigrants, and some of its families will know Altötting by name. He was beatified in 1930, in the abbey's own lifetime, and the label still calls him Blessed.
conrad-of-parzham.relic: One relic in a gilt sunburst (IMG_4977), labelled "B. Konradus à P[arzham]", so written between his beatification in 1930 and his canonization in 1934.

contardo-deste.name: St. Contardo d'Este
contardo-deste.title: Pilgrim, patron of Broni
contardo-deste.summary: St. Contardo d'Este, according to the tradition of Broni in Lombardy, was a son of the house of Este who set out as a poor pilgrim to Compostela and died unknown at Broni in 1249. Broni keeps him as its patron, and Modena as a secondary patron. His story of a stranger recognized too late is a lesson for a house that receives guests.
life: Contardo belonged to the house of Este, the noble family that ruled Ferrara and that also gave the Church the two Blessed Beatrices. Almost all that is told of him comes from local tradition at Broni, a small town near Pavia in Lombardy, and from writers who followed it much later, so the story should be read as a tradition, not as a record.

According to that tradition, Contardo turned his back on his family's wealth and set out as a poor pilgrim to the shrine of St. James at Compostela in Spain, one of the three great pilgrimages of the Middle Ages. He travelled on foot, without money or rank, living on what he was given. On the way he fell gravely ill at Broni. Because no one knew who he was, he was turned away or left with nothing better than a poor shed, and he died there unknown, in 1249, at about thirty-three.

The story goes on that after his death signs were seen at the place, a light and a ringing of bells, and that cures were reported. Only then was it learned that the poor stranger was a son of the house of Este. The townspeople buried him with honor in their church of San Pietro, which later became a basilica, and they have kept him as their patron ever since. Pope Paul V approved the local cult in 1609. Modena, which the Este later ruled, also counts him as a secondary patron.
The label in the abbey's reliquary, "S. Contard. Est.", sits on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este, beside the two Beatrices.
why_here: Contardo's story is about a stranger who is not recognized until too late. That is a sobering lesson for a house that receives guests. The monks at the door, at the Retreat Center and at the Grotto meet pilgrims every day, and they cannot know who any of them is. St. Benedict's answer, to receive every guest as Christ, is what Broni learned too late.

He is also a patron for the journey itself. Many Prep students travel long distances to the school, some from abroad. Pilgrims to the Grotto come from all over, and the abbey's Retreat Center welcomes others on their way. Contardo, who set out poor and did not arrive, is a friend to all who are on the road and to those who fall ill there.
contardo-deste.relic: One relic on the oval of royal saints and saints of the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), labelled "S. Contard. Est."

dominic.name: St. Dominic
dominic.title: Founder of the Order of Preachers
dominic.summary: St. Dominic was a Castilian canon who preached on foot and in poverty in southern France and founded the Order of Preachers, sending his friars to study and preach in the universities and towns. He is a patron of astronomers and of the falsely accused. He is the name saint of Fr. Dominic, the abbey's subprior and a math teacher at the Prep.
life: Domingo de Guzmán was born about 1170 at Caleruega, in Old Castile in Spain. The name on his label, "de Guzmán", is his family name. He studied arts and theology at Palencia for some ten years. His first biographer, Jordan of Saxony, tells that during a famine there he sold his books, precious handwritten copies with his own notes, to feed the poor, saying he would not study on dead skins while living men starved. He became a canon of the cathedral of Osma, living a common life of prayer under the Rule of St. Augustine.

In 1203 and 1205 he travelled north with his bishop, Diego of Osma, on missions for the king of Castile, and passed through Languedoc in southern France. The Albigensian or Cathar heresy had spread there, teaching that the material world was evil. The papal legates sent to answer it came with horses, servants and fine clothes, and won no one. Diego and Dominic told them to preach as the apostles had, on foot and begging their bread. Dominic stayed in the region for about ten years, preaching, debating in public, and in 1206 founded a house at Prouille for women who had left the Cathars. The crusade against the Albigensians, which began in 1209, was a war fought by others, and the later Inquisition was not his work.

In 1215 he gathered a small band of preachers at Toulouse, and in 1216 Pope Honorius III approved them as the Order of Preachers. Dominic did a bold thing. In 1217 he scattered his few friars, sending them to Paris, Bologna, Madrid and Rome, to the universities and the growing towns, to study and preach. He insisted on study as a duty, gave his order a system of elected superiors, and wanted the friars to live poor. He spent the last years of his life on the road. He died at Bologna on 6 August 1221 and was canonized in 1234.

The rosary is linked with his name by long tradition, including a story that Our Lady gave it to him. That is a pious tradition, not a settled historical fact. The prayer grew over centuries, and Dominican friars did much to spread it later on. His friars still keep his motto, to contemplate and to hand on to others the fruits of contemplation.
why_here: Dominic is the name saint of Fr. Dominic, the abbey's subprior and a math teacher at the Prep. A Castilian canon who sent his friars to the universities and made study a part of holiness is a fitting patron for a monk who teaches. Dominic did not think learning and prayer were at odds, and neither does a Benedictine school.

For the students, he is the young man who sold his books to feed the hungry. Study mattered to him, but people mattered more. He also learned that argument wins no one when it comes with pride and comfort, and that the truth is best offered with humility. That is worth knowing for Scholars' Bowl players and debaters, and for anyone who wants to share the faith. Abbey and school keep three relics of him.
dominic.relic: Three relics: a gilt sunburst labelled "S. Dominici de Guzm[an]" (IMG_4890), a theca on the large linen board labelled "S. Dominici C." (of St. Dominic, Confessor), and one label on the oval of fifteen relics (4965).

dymphna.name: St. Dymphna
dymphna.title: Virgin and martyr of Geel
dymphna.summary: St. Dymphna is known only from a 13th-century legend of an Irish princess who fled her father and was killed by him at Geel, in what is now Belgium. What is history is Geel's care for people with mental illness, which grew into a system of family care that still exists. She is patron of those with mental illness, and her prayers can be asked for students who struggle.
life: Dymphna is known to us from a Latin life written in the 13th century, at the request of the bishop of Cambrai, by a canon named Peter. He said he drew on old oral tradition. No earlier record of her survives, so her story is a legend, possibly built on an older cult around two tombs found at Geel, in what is now Belgium. It should be read as a legend.

In the story, Dymphna was the daughter of a pagan king in Ireland and a Christian mother, who had her secretly baptized. When her mother died, the king was wild with grief and wanted to marry a woman just like her. His advisers told him there was none like her except his own daughter. Dymphna, then fourteen, fled across the sea with her confessor, an old priest named Gerebernus, and a few companions, and they settled near Geel. Her father tracked them down. His men killed the priest, and when Dymphna still refused him, the king struck off her head with his own sword.

What is history is Geel itself. A church was built over the relics, and from the Middle Ages people with mental illness were brought there in hope of healing. Records show a sick house beside the church by the 14th century. Pilgrims who stayed for a novena needed lodging, and the townspeople began taking them into their homes. Over the centuries this became a custom and then a system of family care that still exists, in which people with mental illness live as boarders with families in the town, helped by a public psychiatric service. It is often cited as one of the oldest forms of community care in the world.

For that reason Dymphna is the patron of those who suffer from mental illness and of those who care for them. Her feast is kept in Geel and in many places, though she is not in the General Roman Calendar.
patronage: those with mental illness and nervous disorders
victims of abuse within the family
why_here: Depression and anxiety are real among teenagers, and a boarding school, where students live far from home, has to take them seriously. Dymphna is a fourteen-year-old who fled home to escape harm. Her legend is grim, but what grew from it at Geel is good. A whole town took troubled people into its homes and treated them as family. That is exactly the kind of help her intercession points to, prayer alongside real care, never prayer instead of it.

Her prayers can be asked for students and their families, for teachers and dorm staff who notice when someone is struggling, and for anyone in the abbey or the school who carries a hidden burden of mind.
dymphna.relic: One relic on a modern pewter plaque, in the case lined in white linen (IMG_4980).

elizabeth-ann-seton.name: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton
elizabeth-ann-seton.title: Wife, mother, convert, founder of schools
elizabeth-ann-seton.summary: Elizabeth Ann Seton was a New York wife and mother, widowed at twenty-nine, who became a Catholic in 1805 and founded the Sisters of Charity and a school at Emmitsburg, Maryland. She was the first saint born in what is now the United States. She is patron of Catholic schools and widows, and she ran a school for boarders and day pupils, as the Prep does.
life: Elizabeth Ann Bayley was born in New York City in 1774, two years before the Declaration of Independence, into a respected Episcopalian family. Her father was a physician who later served as the city’s health officer. Her mother died when she was three. She grew up devout in her own church, fond of the Psalms and of long walks alone, and was known in New York society for her warmth and good sense.

In 1794 she married William Magee Seton, a young merchant, and they had five children. Within ten years his business had failed and he was sick with tuberculosis. In 1803 the family sailed to Italy in the hope that the climate would help him. On arrival they were held for weeks in a cold quarantine station at Livorno, and William died at Pisa a few days after Christmas. She was twenty-nine, a widow with five small children and no money.

In Italy she stayed with the Filicchi family, friends of her husband, and there she saw Catholic faith lived up close. She was drawn above all by belief in the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist. Back in New York she struggled with the question for more than a year, and in 1805 she became a Catholic, against the wishes of most of her family and friends. Some of them broke with her. She tried to support her children by teaching and keeping a boarding house, with little success.

In 1808 a priest invited her to Baltimore to open a school for girls. The next year she moved to Emmitsburg, Maryland, and with a few companions founded the Sisters of Charity of St. Joseph’s, the first community of religious women founded in the United States. In 1810 they opened St. Joseph’s Academy and Free School, often called the beginning of Catholic parish schooling in the country. She ran the school, trained the teachers, wrote and translated books for them, and went on raising her own children. Two of her daughters died young while she was there.

She died at Emmitsburg on 4 January 1821, at forty-six, of tuberculosis. Her sisters spread across the country and, in several branches, run schools and hospitals to this day. She was beatified in 1963 and canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1975, the first saint born in what is now the United States.
patronage: parents who have lost a child
why_here: Mother Seton ran a Catholic school that took boarders as well as day pupils, and she did it while raising children of her own. That is close to what St. Bernard Prep asks of its teachers and dorm staff, and of the families who send their sons and daughters here. She knew money worries, a sick husband, the death of children and the pain of being misunderstood by her own people. Parents and teachers at the Prep can ask her help with all of those. Students who come to the faith on their own, as she did at thirty, have in her someone who paid a real price for it and did not regret it.
elizabeth-ann-seton.relic: Two relics: one in a gilt sunburst labelled “S.E.A. Seton” (IMG_4886), and one on the grey linen board labelled “Bd. E. A. Seton” (IMG_4933), written while she was Blessed, between 1963 and 1975.

elizabeth-of-hungary.name: St. Elizabeth of Hungary
elizabeth-of-hungary.title: Princess, widow, nurse of the poor
elizabeth-of-hungary.summary: Elizabeth was a Hungarian princess married into the court of Thuringia who gave freely to the poor. Widowed at twenty, she built a hospital at Marburg and nursed the sick there herself until she died at twenty-four, and the roses in her cloak are legend. She is patron of hospitals and nurses, and of the monks who care for the abbey’s old and sick brothers.
life: Elizabeth was born in 1207, a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary. As a small child she was promised in marriage to the son of the Landgrave of Thuringia, in central Germany, and was sent to be brought up at his court, at the Wartburg castle above Eisenach. In 1221, at about fourteen, she married him. Louis was a good and devout man, and by every account the marriage was a happy one. They had three children.

From the start Elizabeth gave food, money and her own time to the poor, so freely that some of her husband’s family objected. During a famine in 1226, while Louis was away, she opened the castle stores, gave out grain, and set up a house below the castle where she cared for the sick herself. Louis backed her when he came home. The well-known story that the bread she carried in her cloak turned to roses when she was challenged is a legend, told later and told of other saints too.

In 1227 Louis set out to join the Emperor’s Crusade and died of fever at Otranto in southern Italy before he could sail. Elizabeth was twenty, with a third child just born. She left the Wartburg, in circumstances that are disputed, and after a hard time settled at Marburg. There she became one of the first Franciscan tertiaries in Germany, wearing a plain grey habit, and used her dowry to build a hospital, dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, who had been canonized the year before.

She worked in it with her own hands, washing and feeding the sick, many of them lepers and the poorest of the town. Her spiritual director, Conrad of Marburg, was a harsh and demanding man, and his treatment of her has troubled readers ever since. She died at Marburg on 17 November 1231, at twenty-four, worn out by the work. Miracles were reported at her grave at once, and she was canonized only four years later, in 1235. The great church built over her tomb at Marburg is one of the first Gothic churches in Germany. Her relics were scattered in the Reformation.
why_here: The abbey keeps an infirmary for its old and sick monks, and its history is marked by men who nursed others at real cost. Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick in the 1878 yellow fever, and Frater Hubert Carney died nursing others in the 1918 flu. Elizabeth did the same work in Marburg, by choice, and it wore her out at twenty-four. She is a good patron for the brothers who care for the infirm, for anyone at the Prep who looks after a sick roommate or a sick parent, and for families who send their children here at some sacrifice. Her German story also belongs naturally in a Bavarian-rooted house.
elizabeth-of-hungary.relic: A theca of her hair on the grey linen board, labelled in Italian “Ex Capil.” and “S. Elisabetta d’ Ung.” (IMG_4920, 4921).

elizabeth-queen.name: St. Elizabeth, Queen
elizabeth-queen.title: Queen of Portugal, peacemaker (most likely)
elizabeth-queen.summary: The labels say only “St. Elizabeth, Queen”, so which Elizabeth is not certain, though Elizabeth of Portugal is the more likely reading. Wife of King Denis, she was known as the peacemaker and once rode between her husband’s and her son’s armies until they made terms. She is patron of peace and peacemakers, a good saint for a monastery and a boarding school.
life: The two labels read “S. Elisabeth R.” and “s. Elisab. Reg.”, that is, “of St. Elizabeth, Queen”. They do not say which Elizabeth, and the two need not be the same saint. The title “Queen” fits St. Elizabeth of Portugal, who was a crowned queen, and one of the labels sits among Spanish royal saints, Ferdinand and Hermenegild. But labels sometimes gave the title to St. Elizabeth of Hungary too, who was a king’s daughter. What follows is the life of Elizabeth of Portugal, the more likely reading.

Elizabeth was born in 1271, a daughter of King Peter III of Aragon, and was named after her great-aunt, St. Elizabeth of Hungary. At about twelve she was married to King Denis of Portugal. Denis was an able king, a poet and a builder, but he was unfaithful to her, and she brought up several of his children by other women along with her own two, Constance and Afonso. She kept a regular life of prayer at court and gave a great deal to the poor, to pilgrims and to hospitals.

Her name in Portugal is the peacemaker. Afonso, her son, quarrelled bitterly with his father, and more than once the quarrel came to open war. In 1323, at Alvalade, the two armies were drawn up to fight when she rode out between them on a mule and would not move until they made terms. She also helped settle disputes between Portugal and Castile and between other Christian kings.

When Denis died in 1325 she made a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela and then lived as a Franciscan tertiary beside the convent of Poor Clares she had founded at Coimbra. In 1336, old and in the summer heat, she travelled to Estremoz to stop a war between her son, now king, and the king of Castile. She fell ill there and died on 4 July. She was canonized in 1625. Her body lies at Coimbra. A story of bread turning into roses is told of her as well as of her great-aunt, and is legend in both cases.
why_here: A monastery is a place where some thirty men have promised to live together for life, and a boarding school is a place where teenagers share rooms, teams and tables with people they did not choose. Both need peacemakers. Elizabeth did not make peace by avoiding conflict. She went and stood between the two sides, at some risk, and refused to leave until they talked. She is a good saint to ask for dorm prefects, for monks with a long-running grudge, for parents and grown children who are not speaking, and for anyone at the Prep who is caught between two friends.
elizabeth-queen.relic: Two relics labelled “of St. Elizabeth, Queen”: “S. Elisabeth R.” in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), and “s. Elisab. Reg.” in the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965).

eucharius.name: St. Eucharius of Trier
eucharius.title: First bishop of Trier
eucharius.summary: Eucharius is counted as the first bishop of Trier, probably in the later third century, though almost nothing about him is known for certain. The story that St. Peter sent him is legend. He is patron of Trier, where Benedictines still keep his tomb, and the relic probably came from there, a sign of the German Benedictine family the abbey belongs to.
life: Trier, on the Moselle in western Germany, was one of the great cities of the late Roman Empire and for a time an imperial capital. Its Church counts Eucharius as its first bishop, with Valerius as his companion and successor and Maternus after them. Historians think he most likely lived in the second half of the third century, when Christianity was spreading along the Rhine and Moselle. Almost nothing else about him is known for certain.

A medieval legend fills the gap. It says that St. Peter himself sent Eucharius, Valerius and Maternus to preach in Gaul, that Maternus died on the way, and that Peter’s staff, sent back with the others, raised him to life. The story was written down centuries later and was meant to give Trier an apostolic founding. It is legend, not history.

Eucharius and Valerius were buried in a cemetery south of the city, and a church and then a monastery grew up over their graves. In the twelfth century the monks found there what they believed were relics of the apostle St. Matthias, and the Benedictine abbey of St. Matthias took its present name. Benedictine monks still live there, and the tombs of the two first bishops are in its crypt.

The relic here was probably part of a gift from Trier. Its reliquary is an exact twin of one labelled “S. Valerio”, in the same jewelled frame and the same red ink and hand, and beside them are a relic of the Martyrs of Trier and one “from the holy relics of the Abbey of St. Matthias”. Who sent them, and when, is not recorded on the labels. If the abbey keeps any letters or authentication papers for this set, they would tell the story.
why_here: If the catalogue’s guess is right, these Trier relics came to Cullman from one Benedictine house to another, perhaps from the monks who keep Eucharius’s tomb to the monks of St. Bernard. That is a small sign of what Benedictine monasteries have always been, separate houses that still belong to one family. St. Bernard was founded from St. Vincent, which was founded from Metten in Bavaria, and the German Catholic roots of the abbey and of Cullman run back to the same Rhineland and Bavarian Church that Eucharius began. His prayers fit a house that remembers where its faith came from.
eucharius.relic: A jewelled gilt reliquary with a faded red-ink label read as “S. Euch[ario]” (IMG_4910, 4911), the twin of the one labelled “S. Valerio”.

eugene.name: St. Eugene
eugene.title: Saint not identified
eugene.summary: The label reads only “S. Eugenii”, so the relic is of a St. Eugene, but which one cannot be said. Candidates include Pope Eugene I, who led the Church of Rome from 654 to 657, and Eugene of Carthage, a bishop exiled for the Catholic faith who died at Albi. If it is the exiled bishop, he is a fitting friend for boarders and monks far from home.
life: The label begins “S. Eugenii…” and the rest is cut off, so the relic is of a St. Eugene, but which one cannot be said. Several saints bore the name. Pope St. Eugene I led the Church of Rome from 654 to 657, chosen while his predecessor, St. Martin I, was still alive in exile, and he died before he could be drawn into the same quarrel with the emperor. St. Eugene of Carthage became bishop there in 480 under the Arian Vandal kings, was exiled with many of his clergy for refusing to give up the Catholic faith, and died in exile at Albi in southern France around 505.

There were others too, among them St. Eugene of Toledo and early martyrs of the name, and relics taken from the Roman catacombs were often given a name like this one. Only the relic’s papers, if they survive, could say which Eugene the abbey has.
why_here: Not knowing which Eugene this is need not stop anyone asking his prayers. If it is Eugene of Carthage, he is a bishop who lost his home and his see for the faith and kept it to the end in a foreign country. That speaks to Prep boarders who are a long way from their families, and to monks who have vowed stability in one place, often far from where they were born. If it is Pope Eugene I, he is a man handed a hard job in a hard time, which is a fair description of many abbots and headmasters.
eugene.relic: A theca on the grey linen board whose label, cut off at the edge of the photo, begins “S. Eugenii…” (IMG_4920).

faustinus.name: St. Faustinus
faustinus.title: Martyr, not identified
faustinus.summary: The label reads “…austini M.”, most likely Faustinus, martyr, but which Faustinus is not known. The best known are Faustinus and Jovita of Brescia and Faustinus of Rome, killed with his brother Simplicius, and their accounts mix history with legend. Both died with a brother, which makes him a fitting saint for monks who call each other brother and for siblings at the Prep.
life: The label reads “…austini M.”, “of Faustinus, martyr”, with the first letter hidden. Several early martyrs bore this name. The best known are Faustinus and Jovita, brothers, put to death at Brescia in northern Italy in the second century and still the patrons of that city (feast 15 February), and Faustinus, martyred in Rome in the persecution of Diocletian with his brother Simplicius, after which their sister Beatrice buried them and was killed in her turn (feast 29 July). The accounts of both pairs were written later and mix history with legend.

Many relics taken from the Roman catacombs in the 1700s and 1800s were also given names like this one, sometimes because a name was found on the tomb and sometimes because one was assigned. Which Faustinus this relic belongs to is not known.
why_here: Both of the best-known martyrs named Faustinus died together with a brother, and one pair had a sister who would not leave them unburied and was killed for it. Whichever Faustinus this is, he is a fitting saint for a house of monks who call each other brother and mean it, and who will one day bury each other in the abbey cemetery. He fits the Prep too, where brothers and sisters sometimes come together, look out for each other far from home, and argue the way siblings do.
faustinus.relic: One of about ten relics in the large oval in the velvet case, labelled “[F]austin[i] M.” (IMG_4894, 4895).

ferdinand-iii.name: St. Ferdinand III
ferdinand-iii.title: King of Castile and León
ferdinand-iii.summary: Ferdinand III united the crowns of Castile and León and spent most of his reign at war with the Muslim rulers of the south, taking Córdoba and Seville. He was also remembered for fair justice, for keeping faith with other Christian kings, and for building, among it Burgos Cathedral. He is patron of rulers and engineers, and of St. Bernard’s builder monks and civics students.
life: Ferdinand was the son of King Alfonso IX of León and of Berenguela of Castile, whose marriage the pope had dissolved because they were too closely related. In 1217 his mother, who had inherited Castile, gave the crown to him. In 1230, when his father died, he became king of León as well, and the two kingdoms were joined for good. Much of what Spain later became begins with that union.

Most of his reign was spent at war with the Muslim rulers of al-Andalus in the south. He took Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and Seville in 1248, after a long siege. These were wars of conquest and should be told as such. He was also known for keeping faith with the other Christian kings and not fighting them, for fair dealing in his courts, and for terms that let many of the conquered people keep their property and their religion.

He was a builder. With the bishop of Burgos he laid the first stone of the Gothic cathedral there in 1221, and the cathedral of Toledo was begun in his reign. He supported the young university at Salamanca. He married twice, to Beatrice of Swabia and after her death to Joan of Ponthieu, and had many children. His eldest son was King Alfonso X, called the Wise, the lawgiver and scholar.

He died at Seville on 30 May 1252. The accounts say he asked to be laid on the ground, received the sacraments with a rope around his neck as a sign of penance, and asked pardon of those around him. He was canonized in 1671, and his body lies in the Royal Chapel of Seville Cathedral. The label “S. Ferdin. R.” means “of St. Ferdinand, King”.
why_here: Ferdinand is remembered less for his battles than for fair justice and for building. The Prep teaches civics, and a king who was praised for keeping his word to his rivals and for judging fairly is a good patron for students learning how a country should be governed. He also stood behind great building work, and the abbey has its own long line of builder monks and carvers. A saint who helped lay the first stone of Burgos Cathedral can be asked to bless the hands of the brothers who still build and repair at St. Bernard, and of students who will go on to be engineers.
ferdinand-iii.relic: One of about fifteen relics in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labelled “S. Ferdin. R.” (IMG_4912–4915).

frances-xavier-cabrini.name: St. Frances Xavier Cabrini
frances-xavier-cabrini.title: Missionary to immigrants
frances-xavier-cabrini.summary: Frances Xavier Cabrini, turned down by two orders as too frail, founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart and in 1889 came to New York to serve Italian immigrants. Her sisters opened schools, orphanages and hospitals across the Americas and Europe. Pius XII named her patron of immigrants, fitting for a town founded by German immigrants and a school with students from abroad.
life: Maria Francesca Cabrini was born in 1850 at Sant’Angelo Lodigiano in Lombardy, the youngest of thirteen children of a farming family, and was born early and small. Only a few of her brothers and sisters lived to grow up. She trained as a schoolteacher and from childhood wanted to be a missionary, but two religious orders turned her down because of her poor health.

A priest sent her instead to help run a struggling orphanage at Codogno. When the bishop closed it, he told her to found her own community, since she wanted to be a missionary and no one else would take her. In 1880 she and a few companions began the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart. She took the name Xavier after St. Francis Xavier and hoped to go to China.

Pope Leo XIII told her to go “not to the East, but to the West”. Millions of Italians were then leaving for the Americas, many to poverty and neglect. In 1889 she landed in New York with six sisters. The archbishop, who had not prepared for them, advised them to go home. She stayed, opened an orphanage, and went on.

Though she had nearly drowned as a child and was afraid of water, she crossed the ocean more than twenty times. Over the next twenty-eight years her sisters opened schools, orphanages and hospitals in the United States, Central and South America and Europe, some sixty-seven houses in all. She was a hard-headed manager of money and buildings. She became a United States citizen in 1909 and died in Chicago on 22 December 1917.
In 1946 Pope Pius XII canonized her, the first citizen of the United States to be declared a saint, and in 1950 he named her patron of immigrants. Her body lies at her shrine in upper Manhattan.
why_here: Cullman is a town founded by German immigrants, and the abbey was founded by their sons and brothers in the faith. The Prep today takes students from across the country and from abroad, some a long way from home in a new language. Mother Cabrini spent her life making a place for people in exactly that position. She is also a saint for anyone who has been turned down. Two orders refused her as too frail, and she did more than either of them expected. And she crossed an ocean she was afraid of more than twenty times. Students facing something they dread can ask her help.
frances-xavier-cabrini.relic: Two relics: one on the grey linen board labelled “S. Franciscae X. Cab[rini]” (IMG_4948), and a clothing relic in the case lined in white linen labelled “Ex Indumentis / Sanctae / F. X. Cabrini” (IMG_4982).

francis-de-sales.name: St. Francis de Sales
francis-de-sales.title: Bishop of Geneva, Doctor of the Church
francis-de-sales.summary: Francis de Sales was bishop of Geneva, a gentle pastor who won back the Chablais with leaflets slipped under doors and wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life for people living in the world. He is a Doctor of the Church, and Pius XI named him patron of writers and journalists. He suits an abbey that publishes its own books, and its oblates.
life: Francis was born in 1567 in the castle of Sales, in Savoy, the eldest son of a noble family. His father meant him for a career in law and public life. He studied with the Jesuits in Paris and took a doctorate in law at Padua. In Paris, as a young man, he went through a long crisis of fear that he was damned, and came out of it by giving himself to the love of God whatever happened. That trust marks everything he later wrote.

Against his father’s wishes he became a priest in 1593. The next year he volunteered to go to the Chablais, on the south shore of Lake Geneva, which had become Calvinist. People would not come to hear him and some tried to kill him. He wrote short leaflets explaining Catholic teaching and slipped them under doors. Over four years much of the region returned to the Catholic Church.

In 1602 he became bishop of Geneva, though Geneva itself was closed to him and he lived at Annecy. He was a careful pastor, preached constantly, and taught the catechism to children himself. His letters of spiritual direction were gathered into Introduction to the Devout Life (1609), written to show that people in the world, married, in business or at court, can be holy where they are. His Treatise on the Love of God followed in 1616. With St. Jane Frances de Chantal he founded the Visitation nuns in 1610.

He was known for gentleness, which he said cost him a long struggle with a quick temper. He died at Lyon in 1622, was canonized in 1665, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1877. In 1923 Pope Pius XI made him patron of writers and journalists, remembering his leaflets. St. John Bosco named his Salesians after him.
why_here: The abbey publishes. Br. Leo edits and reprints its history books, and Br. Augustine keeps its website. Francis de Sales, who won back a region with leaflets pushed under doors, is the obvious saint to ask for clear and charitable writing. He is also a link between two of the monks’ name saints, since St. John Bosco, Fr. John’s patron, named his Salesians after him. And his Introduction to the Devout Life was written for lay people living in the world, which makes it a natural book for the abbey’s oblates and for Prep parents who want a spiritual life that fits a busy one.
francis-de-sales.relic: A theca on the grey linen board labelled “Ex Os. S. Franc. S. Ep.”, most likely “from the bone of St. Francis de Sales, Bishop” (IMG_4958).

francis-of-assisi.name: St. Francis of Assisi
francis-of-assisi.title: Founder of the Friars Minor
francis-of-assisi.summary: Francis, a rich merchant’s son of Assisi, gave up everything, rebuilt ruined chapels with his own hands and founded the Friars Minor to live the Gospel in poverty. He received the stigmata in 1224, and many later stories about him mix history with legend. He is patron of Italy and of ecology, and fits the Grotto’s builder and the monks who work the abbey’s land.
life: Francis was born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182, the son of Pietro di Bernardone, a rich cloth merchant. He was popular and free with money, and dreamed of glory as a knight. In a war with Perugia he was taken prisoner and spent about a year in captivity, then a long time ill. He came home changed, uncertain what he wanted.

Praying in the half-ruined chapel of San Damiano, outside the town, he heard the crucifix tell him to repair God’s house. He took it literally. He sold cloth from his father’s shop to pay for the work, and when his father took him before the bishop, he gave back everything, even the clothes he stood in. He then begged stones and rebuilt San Damiano and two other small churches with his own hands.

Others came to join him. In 1209 or 1210 Pope Innocent III approved their simple way of life, the Gospel lived in poverty, and the brothers went out in pairs to preach, to work and to serve lepers. St. Clare joined him in 1212. In 1219 he went with the Crusaders to Egypt and crossed the lines to speak to the Sultan, who received him courteously. At Greccio in 1223 he set up a living Christmas crib, and on Mount La Verna in 1224 he received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ in his hands, feet and side.

The order grew faster than he could guide it, and his last years were marked by disputes over poverty, by illness and by near-blindness. In that time he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for Brother Sun, Sister Moon and Sister Water. He died at the Porziuncola below Assisi on 3 October 1226 and was canonized two years later. He was never ordained a priest.

Many stories, like his preaching to the birds and taming the wolf of Gubbio, come from collections written after his death. Some are history and some legend. His poverty and his joy are well attested.
why_here: Francis began his conversion by hauling stones and rebuilding a ruined chapel with his own hands. That is very near the spirit of Br. Joseph Zoettl, who built the 125 shrines of the Ave Maria Grotto from stone, shells, glass, marbles and scrap, and of the craftsman monks who came after him. Francis also saw the whole of creation as brothers and sisters. The abbey has more than 800 acres, a garden, beef cattle and some forty chickens, and it remembers Br. Wolfgang Wolf the botanist. Those who work the land and care for the animals here have in Francis a patron who praised God for all of it.
francis-of-assisi.relic: Four relics: “s. Franc. Ass.” in the medallion in the velvet case (IMG_4900), “Ex Cin. S. Franc. As.” on the grey linen board (IMG_4951), “s. Franc. Ass.” in the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965), and “S. Francisci Assisiensis” at the centre of the Gothic reliquary of Franciscan saints (IMG_4970–4972).

francis-xavier.name: St. Francis Xavier
francis-xavier.title: Jesuit, missionary to Asia
francis-xavier.summary: Francis Xavier, a Basque noble, shared rooms with Ignatius of Loyola at Paris and became one of the first Jesuits. He spent his last eleven years as a missionary in India, Malacca and Japan, and died in 1552 waiting to enter China. He is patron of the missions, and a good saint for Prep roommates and for students far from home.
life: Francisco de Jasso y Javier was born in 1506 in the castle of Javier, in Navarre, the youngest son of a noble family that lost much in the wars that brought Navarre under Castile. At nineteen he went to the University of Paris. He was ambitious and meant to make a name for himself in the Church or at court.

At Paris he shared rooms with Peter Faber and with an older Basque student, Ignatius of Loyola. For a long time Francis resisted Ignatius. In the end he made the Spiritual Exercises under him, and in 1534 he was one of the seven who took vows together at Montmartre, the beginning of the Society of Jesus. He was ordained a priest in 1537.

In 1540 the king of Portugal asked for Jesuits for his possessions in India. The man chosen fell ill, and Ignatius sent Francis instead, at a day’s notice. He sailed in 1541 and never saw Europe again. From Goa he worked among the pearl-fishing Paravas on the south coast of India, then in Malacca and the Molucca Islands. He often taught the catechism by setting it to simple tunes and singing it with children in the street, who then taught their parents. In 1549 he reached Japan and spent two years there, learning how much his methods had to change for an old and learned culture.

He then set out for China, which was closed to foreigners. He died of fever on 3 December 1552 on the island of Shangchuan, off the coast, waiting for a ship to take him in. His letters home, read aloud across Europe, drew many young men to the missions. He was canonized in 1622 together with Ignatius. His body lies in Goa and his right arm in the Gesù in Rome.
patronage: missions (Pius XI, 1927, with St. Thérèse of Lisieux)
the Society for the Propagation of the Faith (Pius X, 1904)
why_here: Francis Xavier’s life turned on a friendship made in a student dormitory. He shared rooms at Paris with Ignatius of Loyola, resisted him for years, and was changed by him for good. Prep boarders live in rooms with people they did not choose, and some of the friendships they make here will matter all their lives. He is a good saint to ask for roommates, and for students who are far from home. He left home at thirty-five and never went back, and his letters were what kept him close to his friends.
francis-xavier.relic: Two relics: one in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este (IMG_4912–4915), and one on the grey linen board labelled “Ex Os. S. Franc. Xav. C.”, from a bone of St. Francis Xavier, Confessor (IMG_4939).

gabriel-of-our-lady-of-sorrows.name: St. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows
gabriel-of-our-lady-of-sorrows.title: Passionist student, patron of youth
gabriel-of-our-lady-of-sorrows.summary: Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows was a lively, popular young man of Spoleto who twice promised to enter religious life and put it off, then joined the Passionists at eighteen. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-three, known only for doing ordinary things well. He is patron of young people and students, and a friend to anyone at the Prep or the abbey discerning a vocation.
life: Francesco Possenti was born in 1838 at Assisi, where his father was a government official in the Papal States, and was baptized in the same font as St. Francis. The family soon moved to Spoleto. His mother died when he was four, and several of his brothers and sisters died young. He was schooled by the Christian Brothers and the Jesuits at Spoleto and did well.

He was a lively, good-looking young man who dressed well, loved dancing, hunting and the theatre, and was popular in the town. Twice, when he was seriously ill, he promised God that he would enter religious life if he recovered, and twice he recovered and put it off. In 1855 his sister died of cholera, which shook him.

In August 1856, as an old image of Our Lady was carried past him in procession at Spoleto, he felt that she was calling him to leave the world. This time he went. Over his father’s objections he joined the Passionists, a strict order devoted to the Passion of Christ, and took the name Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows.

His religious life was short and outwardly plain. He studied for the priesthood, kept the rule carefully, was cheerful with his brothers, and had a deep love for Mary in her sorrows. Nothing dramatic is recorded of him. His superiors simply noticed that he did ordinary things very well. In 1859 he was sent to the house at Isola del Gran Sasso in the Abruzzi. There he caught tuberculosis, and he died on 27 February 1862, at twenty-three, before he could be ordained.
Cures were soon reported at his grave. St. Gemma Galgani credited him with her own cure in 1899. He was canonized in 1920, and his shrine at Isola is still visited by great numbers of young Italians.
why_here: Gabriel is a saint who looks a lot like a Prep student. He was clever, sociable, fond of a good time, and slow to follow through on what he knew he should do. When he finally made up his mind at eighteen he gave himself to it completely, and then died at twenty-three having done nothing anyone would call remarkable except live his days well. Students discerning what to do with their lives, and the young men coming to the abbey now that vocations are rising, can ask his help to stop putting off the decision and then to be faithful in small things.
gabriel-of-our-lady-of-sorrows.relic: Two relics: a silver pendant in a gilt Gothic tabernacle labelled “S. Gabrielis a Virg. Perd.” (IMG_4904), and one beside St. Gemma Galgani in a silver almond-shaped frame labelled “S. Gabriel a V. P.” (IMG_4973).

gemma-galgani.name: St. Gemma Galgani
gemma-galgani.title: Mystic of Lucca
gemma-galgani.summary: Gemma Galgani was an orphaned, often sick young woman of Lucca who longed to be a Passionist nun and was never admitted. She lived with a family that took her in, received mystical graces, and died at twenty-five, and she was canonized for her heroic virtue, not her extraordinary experiences. She is patron of students and pharmacists, and a friend to young people whose plans fall through.
life: Gemma was born in 1878 near Lucca, in Tuscany, the daughter of a pharmacist. Her mother, whom she loved deeply, died of tuberculosis when Gemma was eight. She was educated by sisters in Lucca and was a bright and devout pupil. Her father’s business failed, and when he died in 1897 the family was left in poverty. At nineteen she was keeping house for her brothers and sisters.

She was often ill. In 1899 she was gravely sick with what was diagnosed as spinal meningitis, and was expected to die. She made a novena, and said that St. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows came to her during her illness. She recovered suddenly. She longed to enter the Passionist nuns, but her health and other obstacles kept her out, and she was never admitted to any convent.

From 1900 she lived with the Giannini family in Lucca, who took her in as one of their own. She helped in the house and lived quietly. In those years she received extraordinary mystical graces, which were witnessed by the family. Among them were the marks of the stigmata, which appeared at times on her hands and feet, and ecstasies in which she spoke aloud to Jesus. She also suffered what she described as fierce attacks from the devil. Her spiritual director, the Passionist Fr. Germanus Ruoppolo, examined all this cautiously, and after her death wrote her life.

She died of tuberculosis on Holy Saturday, 11 April 1903, at twenty-five. She was beatified in 1933 and canonized in 1940. The Church was careful to say that she was declared a saint for her heroic virtue, her faith, patience, purity and obedience, and not for the extraordinary things reported of her. Her short life is a sign that holiness does not need a long life or a public one.
patronage: those suffering from headaches or back pain
why_here: Gemma wanted one thing, to be a Passionist nun, and never got it. She was sick, poor, orphaned and turned away, and she became a saint anyway in a borrowed room in someone else’s house. That is worth knowing for young people at the Prep whose plans fall through, who are cut from a team, who do not get into the college they wanted, or who live with illness. It is worth knowing for those discerning a vocation too. The abbey keeps one of her relics beside St. Gabriel’s, the young saint she believed had helped her, and the two can be asked together for the young.
gemma-galgani.relic: Three relics: one in a jewelled gilt oval labelled “Gemmae G[algani]” (IMG_4905), one beside St. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows in a silver almond-shaped frame (IMG_4973), and one labelled “Ex Corpore / Gemmae Galgani” in the case lined in white linen (IMG_4978).

gerard-majella.name: St. Gerard Majella
gerard-majella.title: Redemptorist lay brother
gerard-majella.summary: Gerard Majella was a tailor’s son from southern Italy who became a Redemptorist lay brother, working as tailor, gardener and porter. Falsely accused, he kept silent until the charge was withdrawn, and many wonders told of him are hard to sort from legend. He is patron of expectant mothers and the falsely accused, and a friend to the abbey’s working brothers.
life: Gerard was born in 1726 at Muro Lucano in southern Italy, the son of a tailor. His father died when he was twelve, and he was apprenticed to a tailor to support his mother and sisters. He then worked as a servant in the household of a bishop known for his temper, and bore it without complaint. Afterward he set up as a tailor himself, gave much of what he earned to the poor, and spent long hours in prayer.

He tried to join the Capuchins, who turned him away as too frail. In 1749 a group of Redemptorist missionaries came to his town. They too thought him unsuited, and when they left he climbed out of a window and followed them. They took him on trial, and the order’s founder, St. Alphonsus Liguori, later received him as a lay brother. He made his vows in 1752.

As a brother he worked as tailor, gardener, porter and sacristan, and he was sent along on missions, where people were moved by his counsel. In 1754 a young woman he had helped accused him falsely of sin with her. St. Alphonsus questioned him, and Gerard said nothing in his own defence. He was forbidden to receive Communion for a time and accepted it. Some weeks later the woman, seriously ill, took back the charge.

Many stories of wonders were told of him, of reading hearts, of bilocation and of food multiplied for the poor, and they are hard now to sort from legend. One of them is the reason he is asked to pray for mothers. Shortly before he died he left a handkerchief at a family’s house, and years later a daughter of the house, in danger in childbirth, asked for it and came through safely. He died of tuberculosis at Caposele on 16 October 1755, at twenty-nine, and was canonized in 1904.
why_here: Gerard was a tailor and a lay brother who did the plain work of a religious house, mending clothes, keeping the door, tending the garden. St. Bernard has its own brothers doing the same, among them those who do the abbey’s tailoring and keep its grounds, and a saint who made that work holy is a good friend for them. His patronage of expectant mothers reaches the families of the Prep and the faculty, where babies are born every year. And his silence under a false charge is something to remember in a school, where a rumor can travel through the dorms in an hour.
gerard-majella.relic: A theca on the grey linen board labelled “S. Gerardi May[ella] C.” (IMG_4927, 4928).

helena.name: St. Helena
helena.title: Empress, mother of Constantine
helena.summary: Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, came to faith through her son and in old age travelled to the Holy Land, where churches were built at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. Her finding of the True Cross is tradition, not proven history. She is patron of converts and pilgrims, and fits the Ave Maria Grotto with its Holy Land in miniature.
life: Helena was born around 250, probably at Drepanum in Asia Minor, which her son later renamed Helenopolis in her honor. St. Ambrose calls her a stabularia, a stable-keeper or innkeeper’s daughter. She became the companion, and perhaps the wife, of a Roman officer named Constantius, and around 272 she bore him a son, Constantine. When Constantius rose toward the throne he put her aside to marry the emperor’s stepdaughter, and for years she lived in obscurity. The medieval English story that she was a British princess is legend.

Constantine became emperor in 306 and in 312 put the empire under the protection of Christ. He brought his mother to court, honored her, and in 324 gave her the title Augusta. According to the historian Eusebius, who knew the family, she became a Christian through her son, and in old age she was devout, generous to the poor and to prisoners, and often seen praying among ordinary people in church.

In about 326, when she was nearly eighty, she travelled to the Holy Land. Eusebius records that churches were built at Bethlehem, over the cave of the Nativity, and on the Mount of Olives in her time and with her support. She died soon after her return, probably around 330, with her son beside her.

The story that she found the True Cross in Jerusalem first appears in writing in a sermon of St. Ambrose in 395, some sixty years after her death. Later versions add the nails of the Crucifixion. This is tradition, not proven history, though it was quickly and widely believed. Her empty porphyry coffin is in the Vatican Museums, and several churches, in Rome and elsewhere, claim her body. The label “Oss. S. Hel. Imp.” means “from the bones of Saint Helena, Empress”.
why_here: Helena went to the Holy Land as an old woman to see and honor the places where Christ lived and died. Br. Joseph Zoettl never made that journey, but he built the Holy Land in miniature at the Ave Maria Grotto, and visitors still walk past his small Jerusalem and Bethlehem. The abbey also keeps a relic labelled from the Holy Nail, which tradition ties to Helena’s search in Jerusalem. She is a fitting patron for the Grotto and its pilgrims. She came to faith late, after a hard life and a broken marriage, and she can be asked for parents of students who are converts or who carry family hurts of their own.
helena.relic: Two relics: “Oss. S. Hel. Imp.” on the grey linen board (IMG_4944, 4945), and “s. Helenae Im.” in the large oval of fifteen relics (IMG_4965).

henry-ii.name: St. Henry II
henry-ii.title: Emperor, patron of Benedictine oblates
henry-ii.summary: Henry II, Duke of Bavaria and later emperor, reformed the Church, supported the reforming monks and founded the diocese of Bamberg. A tradition says an abbot accepted his vow of obedience and then sent him back to rule. Pius X named him patron of Benedictine oblates, which makes him the patron of the abbey’s own oblates and of all who live the Rule outside the cloister.
life: Henry was born in 973, the son of Henry, Duke of Bavaria, called the Quarrelsome, who rebelled more than once against his cousins the emperors. The boy was educated at the cathedral school of Hildesheim and at Regensburg under its bishop, St. Wolfgang, a former monk, who gave him a lasting love for the Church and its monasteries. In 995 he succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria.

In 1002 he was elected king of Germany, and in 1014 Pope Benedict VIII crowned him emperor in Rome. He spent much of his reign at war, against rebels at home and against the Poles, Italians and others, and he could be a hard ruler. He also worked steadily to reform the Church. He chose able bishops, called synods, and supported the reforming monks who were renewing the abbeys of the empire.

In 1007 he founded the diocese of Bamberg in Franconia and built its cathedral, where he and his wife, St. Cunegund, are buried. They had no children. A later legend says they lived as brother and sister by agreement. It is not known whether that is true.

A story told of him says that when he visited the abbey of Saint-Vanne at Verdun, he asked to stay and become a monk. The abbot, Richard, accepted him, took his vow of obedience, and then ordered him, under that obedience, to go back and govern the empire as before. The story was written down after his death and should be taken as tradition, but it is the reason Benedictines have long claimed him as one of their own.

He died in 1024 and was canonized in 1146 by Pope Eugene III, the Cistercian disciple of St. Bernard of Clairvaux. Pope St. Pius X named him patron of Benedictine oblates. The label “S. Henrici R.” means “of St. Henry, King”.
why_here: St. Bernard Abbey has oblates, lay men and women attached to the monastery who live by the Rule of St. Benedict in their own homes and work, and Br. Benedict directs them. St. Henry is their patron. The story of Verdun says exactly what an oblate is. He wanted to be a monk, he promised obedience, and he was sent back to his own life to live it as a monk would. He was a Bavarian, like the founders of Metten, and he was canonized by a pupil of St. Bernard. Oblates, and Prep parents and alumni who try to keep a Benedictine way of life outside the cloister, have in him a patron who knew how hard that is.
henry-ii.relic: One of about fifteen relics in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labelled “S. Henrici R.” (IMG_4912–4915).

hermenegild.name: St. Hermenegild
hermenegild.title: Visigothic prince and martyr
hermenegild.summary: Hermenegild was a Visigothic prince in Spain who became a Catholic through his wife and St. Leander, then revolted against his Arian father. Captured, he refused communion from an Arian bishop at Easter 585 and was put to death. He is usually named patron of converts, and he is a good saint for young people who must hold to their conscience under pressure.
life: In the sixth century Spain was ruled by the Visigoths, a Germanic people who held the Arian belief that the Son is not fully God, while most of the people they ruled were Catholic. Hermenegild was the elder son of King Leovigild, a strong and successful ruler who wanted one kingdom with one faith, and that faith Arian.

In 579 Hermenegild married Ingund, a Frankish princess and a Catholic, who refused to give up her faith even under pressure from the queen. His father sent the couple to govern Seville. There, through his wife and through the bishop, St. Leander of Seville, Hermenegild became a Catholic himself, and he took the name John.

He then rose in revolt against his father and set himself up as king in the south. It is not clear how far the revolt was about religion and how far about power, and historians still argue. The Spanish chronicler John of Biclaro and the Frankish historian Gregory of Tours, writing in his own time, saw him as a rebel. After several years of war Leovigild took Seville in 584, captured his son, and sent him into prison at Tarragona.

Pope St. Gregory the Great, writing a few years later, tells the rest. At Easter in 585 an Arian bishop was sent to give Hermenegild communion and so bring him back to his father’s faith. He refused, and he was put to death in his cell. Gregory saw him as a martyr. Within two years Leovigild was dead, and Hermenegild’s brother, King Reccared, became a Catholic and in 589 brought the Visigothic kingdom into the Catholic Church. Gregory took that as the fruit of his brother’s death. The label “S. Hermeneg. R.” means “of St. Hermenegild, King”.
why_here: Hermenegild’s story is not a simple one, and it should not be told as one. He took up arms against his own father, and that is not to be admired. But at the end, alone in a prison cell, he was offered his freedom for one act against his conscience and would not do it. That is a choice many young people face in smaller ways, under pressure from friends, a team or a family. Students who have come to the faith on their own, or who hold to it while others at home do not, can ask his help to be firm without being hard.
hermenegild.relic: One of about fifteen relics in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labelled “S. Hermeneg. R.” (IMG_4912–4915).
hermenegild.credit: Francisco Herrera the Younger · Public domain

innocent.name: St. Innocent
innocent.title: Saint not identified
innocent.summary: The label names one St. Innocent but does not say which. The best known is Pope Innocent I, who led the Church of Rome from 401 to 417 and through the sack of Rome by the Goths, but the relic may belong to an early martyr known only by name. Whoever he is, he can be asked for those who lead the abbey and the school through hard years.
life: The label “Oss. S. Innocent.” means “from the bones of Saint Innocent”. The “S.” is singular, so it is one saint named Innocent, not the Holy Innocents, the children killed by Herod, who would be written “SS.”. Several saints bore the name. The best known is Pope St. Innocent I, who led the Church of Rome from 401 to 417. He was away at Ravenna, trying to make peace, when the Goths under Alaric sacked Rome in 410. He confirmed the African bishops’ condemnation of Pelagius at the request of St. Augustine and his fellow bishops, and he defended St. John Chrysostom when he was driven from Constantinople.

There were also a number of early martyrs named Innocent, among them a soldier of the Theban Legion, and some known only from a name on a tomb in the Roman catacombs. Relics from the catacombs, given out from Rome in the 1700s and 1800s, often bore names of this kind. The label does not say which of them this is.
why_here: If this is Pope Innocent I, he led the Church when Rome itself fell to the Goths, a disaster that shook the whole Christian world, and he kept working for peace and for sound teaching. It was that same disaster that moved St. Augustine, Br. Augustine’s patron, to write The City of God, and the two men worked together against the teaching of Pelagius. But the label may just as well belong to a martyr whose name is all that is left. Whoever he is, he can be asked for those who lead the abbey and the school through hard years.
innocent.relic: A theca on the grey linen board labelled “Oss. S. Innocent.” (IMG_4943, 4944).

jacinta-and-francisco-marto.name: Sts. Jacinta and Francisco Marto, and the Fatima tree
jacinta-and-francisco-marto.title: Shepherd children, seers of Fatima
jacinta-and-francisco-marto.feast: 20 February (where kept; not on the General Roman Calendar)
jacinta-and-francisco-marto.summary: Francisco and Jacinta Marto were shepherd children of Fatima who, with their cousin Lúcia, said a lady from heaven appeared to them in 1917. Both died young of influenza, and they were canonized for how they lived, not for what they saw. Popular devotion asks their prayers for sick children and for peace, and they show the Prep's youngest students that holiness does not wait for adulthood.
life: Francisco and Jacinta Marto were brother and sister, the youngest children of a farming family in Aljustrel, a hamlet in the parish of Fatima in central Portugal. Like most children of the village they could not read, and they spent their days minding the family's sheep with their older cousin, Lúcia dos Santos. Francisco was quiet and liked to be alone. Jacinta was lively and quick to cry.

In 1917 the three children said that a lady from heaven appeared to them over a small holm oak (in Portuguese azinheira) at the Cova da Iria, a hollow where they grazed the sheep. She came on the 13th of each month from May to October, except in August, when the local administrator held the children and the meeting took place a few days later elsewhere. Lúcia later wrote that the lady asked them to pray the rosary every day, to pray and make sacrifices for sinners, and to pray for peace. Francisco saw the lady but did not hear her words. On 13 October a large crowd said they saw the sun spin and plunge. The children were questioned, threatened and doubted, and people came by the thousands. Within months pilgrims had stripped the little tree bare for keepsakes.

The two younger children took the message to heart in different ways. Francisco spent hours praying alone, wanting, as he put it, to console the hidden Jesus in the tabernacle. Jacinta was moved most by the thought of sinners and gave up food and water on hot days for them. Both caught the influenza that swept Europe after the First World War. Francisco died at home on 4 April 1919, not yet eleven. Jacinta suffered for months, was taken to a hospital in Lisbon, and died there alone on 20 February 1920, aged nine. Lúcia became a nun and lived until 2005.

The bishop of Leiria approved the apparitions in 1930 as worthy of belief. That is approval of a private revelation. It means the Church finds nothing in it against faith and allows devotion to it, but no Catholic is bound to believe it. The holiness of the two children is a separate matter, judged by their lives. John Paul II beatified them at Fatima in 2000, and Pope Francis canonized them there on 13 May 2017. They are the youngest saints who were not martyrs.
